On the Orders of the Day being called:
Mr. 0. TURGEON: Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I beg to call the attention of the Prime Minister and of the Government to the calamity which

befell the fishermen of Caraqnet and Ship-pigan on Friday last during the terrible storm. At first I thought that perhaps only a few individual eases of loss would be reported, but later reports show that it has been a real disaster, and that numbers of families are left to-day without a breadwinner, both father and son having been taken away from mother and children; and the Caraquet fishing fleet is crippled ae to its operations for the present season of navigation, as perhaps one-third or one-quarter of the vessels have been either broken up or dismantled. It is a -case which calls for the assistance of the Government. I believe lit is true that not only the Gloucester fishermen but those of Gaspe and Bonaventure have suffered severely, but from all accounts the Caraquet fishing fleet appears to have suffered the greatest in the number of lives and the amount of property lost. I appeal to the Government under these circumstances, because it is a calamity that has touched a portion of the most valiant people in New Brunswick, who take each year from the sea a yield of fish that contributes immensely to the wealth of the province. We have on some occasions voted money, very properly, and none too generously, in my opinion, for the fishermen, say, of Newfoundland, and for the sufferers in the recent disaster to the Empress of Ireland; but, as this is a case in which a whole county, with the pursuit of generations, is affected, it merits the attention of the Government; and I hope that the Prime Minister and his colleagues, especially the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, whom I see in his seat, will be impressed with the necessity of voting a sum of money appropriate to the exigencies of the circumstances.
It is one of those disasters which cannot be explained. For the last fourteen years not one life has been lost in the fishing fleet of Gloucester which numbers about 8,900 men. The storm came without warning. I do not wish to impute any fault to the keepers of signals. I know that our fishermen pay serious attention to any signal that may be given. But the reports say that the storm came without warning, in the midst of the darkness, and was accompanied by a fall of snow, which no one expected on the 4th of June. I hope the Government will take this matter into serious consideration and vote an amount adequate to the circumstances I e-fore Parliament prorogues.

Early this imoming,
when my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, quite naturally, had left the House, I drew the attention of the Minister of Marine to the very severe storm which had occurred on the coast of Bonaventure and Gaspe, and I repeat what I said during the night that it seems to me that the Government should come to the rescue of the unfortunate families who have been bereaved. I understand from a letter I have received that about twenty-five fishermen on the coasts of Gaspe and Gloucester have perished.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter referred to by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Tur-geon) was brought to the attention of the House at an early hour this morning by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux),whentheEstimatesof ,my department were under consideration. That hon. gentleman understood therehad been a loss of life on the Gaspe coast of something like twenty. I may say that since the hon. gentleman brought that matter to my attention, I have received a letter from Mr. A. J. H. Stewart, a member of the New Brunswick Legislature, in which he states that the loss of life is over 100, including the loss of life in Quebec and New Brunswick. Further than that, he says that in a number of cases at least tbe houses of the fishermen have been destroyed by the force of what was a cyclone, so that in many cases families have not only been deprived of their breadwinner, but of their homes as well.	.
I understand that this cyclone came without a moment's warning. Whether or not there was any weakness in the signal service I do not know, but from information we have at present I am disposed to think that it was one of those unforeseen events that no human agency could have guarded against. My attention was called to this letter of Mr. Stewart's last night, just after the House adjourned. I had a night message sent to a gentleman in Caraquet, Mr. Fred Young, asking him if he could give us information regarding the extent of the disaster that we could rely upon. I am waiting for that information now.
The difficulty about asking Parliament for a vote now is that we have not at the present time sufficient information to enable the Government to come to an adequate conclusion as to what amount of aid they should give, if they give any aid at all. Unless we can get further particulars re-

garding the extent of the disaster, we might be giving too little aid, or too much. I hope, however, we shall have information upon which an intelligent conclusion may be arrived at in the course of a few days, and if the information does not come in time to ask for a vote at this session, perhaps the matter can be dealt with by a Governor General's warrant, if the Government, with all the facts before them, consider that aid should be given to relieve the suffering entailed upon those left behind on account of the disaster.
The disaster is, no doubt, a very great one. In all my experience I have never known of such a calamity in the province of New Brunswick; and I am sure that the hon. member for Gloucester has the sympathy of every one here, and that the sympathy of the whole country will go out to these fishermen; and we all trust that later reports will show that the disaster is not so great as it would appear to be from those we have received up to the present time.

I appreciate very sincerely the sympathetic remarks of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and as the time before the closing of Parliament is very limited, I might say to the hon. minister that, in a matter of urgency like this any amount appropriated by the Government after Parliament closes will certainly receive the sanction of Parliament at the next session.

speechtext: The matter brought to the attention of the Government by my hon. friends from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) and Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) is one worthy of careful consideration. To provide for the expenses of commission to prepare plans relating to the cities of Ottawa and Hull, $55,000.
['No, they are not.\nResolutions reported.']
Has the minister any explanation of this?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is aware
that the Government, acting jointly with the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull, has appointed a commission for the purpose of drawing up a plan looking to the future development of the cities of Ottawa and1 Hull. The commission consists of Mr. H. S. Holt, of Montreal, who is chairman; Sir Alexander Lacoste; Mr. R. Home Smith apd Mr. Frank Darling, of the city of Toronto; and the mayors of the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull, ex-officio. The commission is engaged at present in the preparation of a plan. The estimate now undep consideration provides for an expenditure of $55,000, made up as follows: Engineering, office rent, adtninistrative services and drafting, $27,160; engineering consultation and expenses, $26,000; architectural office administration and drafting, $17,500; architectural consultation and expenses, $7,500; the commissioners' expenses 'to and from Ottawa, $1,200; making a total of $55,960. The work for the year will consist of the continuation and completion of general surveys and surveys of specific details as to city plans, maps and data; also an analysis of ultimate administration required and floor space in buildings, both government and civic. Further, an analysis of the street system with a view to the recommendation of improvements. The commission have also under consideration the de-

velopment of a general plan of the city and the surrounding country, a study of the park system, a study of the transportation system and the preparation of drawings illustrating the developments suggested. Considerable work was done during the year ending March 31, the commissioners having ibeen appointed in October last. After the commission was appointed officials were retained and engaged and lines of study were laid out. Prior to the appointment of the commission a contour-map was prepared by Mr. Cauchon on the scale of 400 feet to the inch and a plan, 1,200 feet to the inch, of Ottawa and surrounding country on the Ontario side. The consulting and landscape architect and town-planner is Mr. E. H. Bennett, of Chicago. The consulting engineer is Mr. E. L. Cousins, of Toronto; the assistant engineer, Mr. A. E. K. Bunnell. In addition, there are four draughtsmen, seven surveyors and an assistant secretary. Offices have been retained and axe now occupied in the Booth building here.

I am not sure that the plan proposed toy my hon. friend is the best one possible, but I do not propose to offer any objection except in one respect. The gentlemen who have been appointed to the commission are certainly very excellent men, most of them eminent in their professions; tout I doubt if men actively engaged in business will have the leisure to devote to this work which it really requires. I would prefer my hon. friend to have selected men not actively engaged in business, but having, of course, great experience in matters of this kind. It may be that my criticism is inopportune. If the results, however, are -such as my hon. friend anticipates, he will be justified in the selection he has made. Up to the present time I understand that no work has been done. The only practical thing that has been accomplished is the preparation of a contour map of Hull and Ottawa. If there is such a plan, it would be interesting to have a copy laid on the table of the House for the benefit of those who take an interest in the matter. Who is the permanent engineer in charge of this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Cousins is the permanent consulting engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have told my right hon. friend that Mr. Cousins is in general charge. It is not necessary for him to be here every day. If he were, the cost would be very much more than $27,000. It is not necessary to have a resident engineer in charge of the work of preparing the surveys and plans. The engineer in the first place outlines a course to be followed toy his assistants, and he can see from time to time how the work is going on. It would only increase the expenses to instruct an ex-

pensive engineer to remain in Ottawa all the time.

I understand
this office is managed from the city of Toronto, and I do not think that is the proper way of doing it. I think my hon. friend should have an engineer at Ottawa in charge of the work, to see that it is properly executed. This commission is composed of gentlemen who nearly all reside outside of Ottawa, and I do not think we shall get value for our money; 'but that remains to he seen. They have not made a report up to the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. My right hon. friend evidently overlooks the fact that this commission is engaged in an extensive work which will occupy them for a considerable length of time. The scheme is very comprehensive and far-reaching, and a great deal of data has to be compiled before the work of actually preparing the plan can be commenced. My hon. friend has referred to the personnel of the commission. ' It seems to me that we could not have selected more capable men. Mr. Holt is one of the most energetic business men of Canada. He is one of those men who, when they take up a thing pursue it to the end, and I have no doubt that he will perform his duties creditably both to himself and the Government. Sir Alexander Lacoste is well known in Montreal, and I do not think any exception can be taken to him. Mr. R. Home Smith, of Toronto, has had very great experience in the laying out of real estate, and has good judgment with regard to town planning. He has taken considerable interest in the matter of town planning for the city of Toronto. Mr. Frank Darling, of Toronto, is one of the most eminent architects in Canada. t In addition, the cities of Hull and Ottawa are both represented by their mayors. The Dominion Government will pay half the cost of the preparation of this plan, and the cities of Ottawa and Hull will pay in proportion to their population. It takes some time to get work of this kind under way. I do not think that expensive engineers should give up their whole time to a matter of this kind, especially at the inception of the work. The first thing to be done was to obtain a contour map of Ottawa and its environs, and that was done over a year ago. It is now available for the commission, which will make use of the information contained in that map. Officials are now at work obtaining further necessary information as to the amount of

floor and office space in the city of Ottawa which it is expected the Dominion Government will require in the future having regard to the probable growth of the Dominion. All that is by way of compilation, and will be available before the actual work of plotting the plan is started. If there is one thing I have been impressed with, it is the energy and expedition with which the commission has taken up this work. Immediately upon Mr. Holt's appointment he made a visit to Minneapolis and certain other cities for the purpose of gathering information to assist him in the discharge of his duties. The others have been at Ottawa on various occasions, and there is no question that the office here is organized on a business basis and is doing efficiently work which it was designed to carry out.

I have nothing to say against the commissioners who have been selected. Mr. Holt in particular is a very able man, but though an able man, he is a still more busy man. I have my doubts whether Mr. Holt will be able to give the attention which should be given to the work of this undertaking. If he can give the attention to it I am sure the work will be well done. I do not know whether Sir Alexander Lacoste can give his time to the work or not; I have no information about that. As to the other two gentlemen, I do not know that I can say anything. But, my hon. friend will permit me to say that if he thinks he can have this work done without anybody to supervise it he will find that he is making a mistake. He may call that business, but I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend puts into my mouth what I did not say. My right hon. friend has said that these gentlemen are busy men. So they are, but my experience has been that busy men find time to do things, and that they are more likely to find time than men of the leisured class. My right hon. friend has expressed a preference for those not actually engaged in business, or those who have retired. I think he might have his hands full in finding retired men capable of doing this work as well as the members of the present commission. I have here a report from the mayor of the city of Ottawa under date of April 28 of this year-and it must not be lost sight of that the cities of Ottawa and Hull are represented by their mayor upon this commission. I have heard no com-complaint, except from my right hon

I read in the press yesterday that Mr. Holt was resigning from many boards of trade because of his numerous occupations in various fields. If, indeed, Mr. Holt is resigning in order to give more time to this commission, I dare say that a better choice than my hon. friend has made could not be made. But I doubt that Mr. Holt is resigning from so many boards for the purpose of devoting all his attention to the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly Mr. Holt is not resigning for the purpose of giving his entire time to this commission, because his entire time is not necessary. In the Senate the other day a question was put by the Hon. "Senator Power, of Halifax, as to the rate of interest on deposits in the post office savings banks. Does my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) think that in the present financial condition he would not be doing well by increasing the rate of interest on the savings in the post office savings banks? There is a general outcry amongst the plain people of this country against the low rate of interest the Government pays its depositors. Could not my hon. friend take t!ie interests of the plain people to his heart, and pro bono publico increase the rate of interest paid to depositors in the post office savings banks by one per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter has frequently been discussed in the House. The raising the interest rate on savings deposits in the post office, and in the chartered banks of the Dominion, would be followed by an increase in the discount rate. If my hon. friend had taken the trouble that I have to look into this matter, and had examined the statement of, say, the Bank of Montreal, he would have found that to increase the rate of interest by even one half of one per cent would have a very serious effect on the earning power of that institution. The result would be to increase the discount

rate to the manufacturers and business people of Canada.
The discount rate has been increased already.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In certain places; hut the average discount rate has not been increased. After all, I think this matter should be approached in a business way. We should look at the statements of the banks, not of one particular bank or even two or three, but of the banks as a whole. The Bank of Montreal is of course the greatest financial institution in Canada, and its balance sheet affords evidence that an increase in the rate upon its savings deposits would have a very considerable influence upon its earnings, so much so, that the inevitable result would be an increase in the discount rate not only in the case of the Bank of Montreal, but as regards every bank in the country. This question has been before other Ministers of Finance, and I think they have reached substantially the same conclusion. For the present, at all events, I see no prospect of increasing the interest rate on deposits in the post office savings banks. I may say that my predecessor reduced the interest rate on such deposits, giving as his reason that in consequence of its being an artificial rate the discount rate had been found burdensome to business. I believe in giving to depositors what their money is worth; but money on call, or practically on call, never obtains the rate of interest which is obtained on money that is left for a period of years. I may say further, that in estimating the rate of interest paid to depositors in the post office savings banks, certain items of expense have to be taken into account. In the first place, 10 per cent of the gold reserve must toe maintained. Gold is barren, and consequently the rate of interest, instead of toeing 3 per cent, becomes 3 1-3 per cent. Next, the cost of administration must be added, bringing the rate in excess of 3i per cent. As I have pointed out, the interest rate which can be obtained on money which is not to be called for until the end of a period of years, is always higher than the rate of interest paid on money practically on call.
Are post office savings deposits increasing?

I do not want my toon, friend to toe disturbed by the sight of this memorandum I have in my hand, but I wish to say a few words on the question of tobacco growing. This memorandum is in French, but, as my hon. Mend is a good French scholar, he will be able to understand it, and can think over it at his five o'clock tea. It was sent to me toy the electors of Rouville county. They claim that the Minister of Agriculture has neglected this question of tobacco growing 'in the county I represent. I will read what it says:
It is easy to realize by comparison between the reports appearing as appendices in the minister's reports (1907-1912) and the short note contained in the minister's report (1913, page 36), the relative importance attributed to the tobacco service since it was connected with the experimental farm service (January, 1913).
On the other hand, it may be judged by the notes on tobacco growing which were picked out of the reports made by the horticulturist (19041905) as to whether it was time that the work towards improvement and development, undertaken since 1896, should be entrusted to a service specialized in this branch of the farming industry.
The series of bulletins published by the tobacco service (No. A-l to No. A-14) gives an idea of the mass of information which was put within the reach of the tobacco planters in Canada.
For the last few years, up to July, 1912, those bulletins were published in the shape of reports, mentioning in detail the work effected at the experimental stations and laying stress upon the results which had been achieved. It is found that those reports were published shortly after the fiscal year had expired, whereas the report from the experimental farms is forwarded to the public but a long time after.
On the other hand, it may be noticed that the appendix to the minister's report having reference to tobacco growing was not limited to mentioning the results obtained during the season, but was somewhat a comment upon those same results, and at the same time, an outline of a programme. Nothing similar is to be found in the reports, forcibly shortened for want of

space, which were published since the year 1912 has come to an end.
The previous organization, in the shape of a branch under the direct control of the minister, offered the following advantages:
It did away with the very long delays in the publication of the reports;
It made the questions under consideration more important in the opinion of the chief of the service (these latter being put forcibly into the background, in an organization so comprehensive as that of the experimental farms) and even in the opinion of the minister, with whom the chief of the service could communicate directly, laying stress, if need be, upon certain particular points the interest of which can escape anybody else than a specialist;
It gave this latter a freer hand, he being not obliged to follow the ways of a complicated organization, many branches of which have no relation to the tobacco industry ;
It made the execution of the work more rapid, which is of great moment when one has to deal with a crop occupying the soil for so short a time as does the tobacco plant, and with a service comparatively new and not yet completely established, and liable to very numerous emergencies;
It made the responsibility entirely incumbent on a specialist conversant with all the phases of the industry to be developed.
An instance of the efficiency of the previous organization is afforded by the rapid transformation which was brought about with respect to the type of tobaccos grown at Saint-C6saire since the possibility of using those tobaccos in the manufacture of cigars has been demonstrated to the manufacturers in Montreal and Quebec. Tobaccos which sold regularly at 7 or 8 cents a pound went up as high as 15 cents, and this advance was portioned out on all the tobaccos in the province of Quebec.
It must be noted that the organization in the shape of a branch would not be more costly than the organization in the shape of a division.
It looks strange that, after the organization and the development of a service to a certain extent has been allowed, its importance should be reduced the moment certain questions relating to the tobacco industry itself seem to become more serious and more complicated.
The farmers in Ontario have shown, during last winter, how dissatisfied they were with the treatment which is meted out to them by the manufacturers. The planters in Quebec are just about as dissatisfied and the co-operative of Saint-C6saire has undergone, recently, a serious crisis.
It seems desirable that a more complete organization, especially as far as the number of inspectors is concerned, should be established under no delay. The Canadian planters are beginning to realize that they must look to the Department of Agriculture for a chance of success, and with that purpose in view, it is necessary that they should come into the closest contact possible with them.
If we consider that the operation, very simple in appearance, of desiccating a crop of tobacco, requires, in certain cases (drying by fire -drying by hot air) expert specialist, we fully realize that this is a real industry, a farming industry, evidently, but one which is clearly specialized. The very difficulty which is experienced in securing experts conversant enough with just one of those processes proves the fact to evidence.
As for the other phases in the curing of tobacco, the sorting and the fermentation, they have practically nothing to do with the growing, and when we realize their importance and the different treatments which they imply, we see how logical it would be to re-establish a branch devoted exclusively to the study of those different questions. Let us add that, among the problems to be solved, the most important are, perhaps, those relating to the organization of the planters in view of the curing and of the sale of their produce.
It is only fair to admit that the tobacco industry in Canada-especially the part of this industry which depends really upon the home production-cannot be compared, for its importance, say with the animal industry or the dairy industry. However, the complexity of the problems to be solved, the wideness of the scope to be covered in the domain of practical farming and practical industry, as well as in the domain of research, for it must be borne in mind that the growing of tobacco in Canada is done under very special climatic conditions-all this would seem to justify, on the part of the service appointed to improve and to develop this industry, a broader initiative as well as a complete responsibility.

I want to call the attention of the Minister of Labour to a matter that has been brought to my attention by a gentleman in the town of Truro, who has taken some interest in the comparative prices paid for labour, and also in' the hours of service required in connection with public works in various parts of Canada He has gone very thoroughly into the matter; and I notice, in a circular letter which he has issued, that in the town of Truro

and I presume in the eastern section of Canada- men are required to work for nine or ten hours a day n Government works, whereas in the province of British Columbia they are required to work for only eight hours a day. Has that matter been brought to the attention of the minister?

My attention has not been called to the condition nor to the letter to which my hon. friend refers; but I know that the wages paid vary in different parts of the country, just as the wages paid by contractors vary.

I understand that, because the wages would be regulated by the fair-wage schedule. What about the hours
of service?

The number of hours varies also. When we make up a schedule, we ascertain the wages paid in the district to the different classes of labour, and also the number of hours of work. The men work sometimes for eight, sometimes nine and sometimes ten hours a day. Then we make up the schedule according to the conditions in the district in which the work is to be done.

I do not think it is fair to ask a man to work for nine hours a day in the Maritime provinces where he receives less pay than he does in British Columbia where he has to work for only eight hours. There is no law in* Canada governing the hours of labour; and I can understand that in certain trades the men have, by virtue of the strength of their unions, an eight-hour day. In the eastern part of the province, for instance in the city of Sydney-I will mot speak for Truro, because I do not know about conditions
in that town-and in the city of Halifax the carpenters work for only eight or eight and a half hours a day. I understand that there is legislation governing the rate of wages paid under a contract, namely, that the rate is governed by the rate of wages paid in the district in which the work is being carried on; but I do not think it should hold good in regard to the hours, there being no law governing the matter. The minister might investigate the matter during the summer and see if he does not agree with me in regard to it.

Can the Minister of
Labour give me any information as to the trouble that existed last year between the Harbour Commissioners and the carpenters at Montreal? Is anything being done to settle the trouble that was in existence before the minister's trip to England?

Two weeks ago we took that .matter up with the members of the Montreal Harbour Commission; and the acting chairman at that time agreed that, if there were any complaints made by the carpenters working for the harbour commissioners, he would be very glad to take the matter up with our fair-wage officer tnd fo do everything possible to make things satisfactory to the men. Many complaints have been made in that respect for years; we have from time to time sent the fail wage officer, Mr. Dubreuil, to Montreal to arrange matters with	the	Board
of Harbour Commissioners, and he has generally succeeded	in adjusting them to the satisfaction of the men. A few months ago he did not succeed; the matter was taken up with the acting chairman of the harbour commissioners by one of the ministers, and the chairman undertook to meet the fair wage officer at any time that complaints were made and to do everything possible to meet his requests.

If I understand the
minister aright, what he says now is not in regard to the past, but for the future. What transpired last year is still pending. I do not suppose the carpenters have received any satisfaction. I know that the minister, before his trip to England, told the harbour men that, on his return, he would do everything possible to settle the question.
I want the minister's interpretation of the fair-wage clause. If my memory is
* 

correct, I believe he has already given an interpretation of that clause to the labour men of Montreal. For instance, suppose a contract is let with the fair-wage clause attached thereto, and suppose wages increase ini the different trades during the operation of that contract, will the contractor be compelled, under the contract he has signed with the Government, to pay that increase?

That would depend
altogether upon the wording of the contract. We have had different forms' of contract, some of them containing a minimum wage and also a general clause, the general clause providing that the contractor would have to pay the current rate of wages even if it was above the minimum rate fixed in the schedule. Wherever there has been a clause of that kind in the contract, we have insisted upon the contractors following the wages, and, if they increase, paying whatever the current rates of wages are. In some of the contracts there has been no such thing as a general clause of that character, simply a minimum clause. I brought before the Government, before I was laid away for a while, the matter of providing for a uniform provision in all the contracts touching labour, so that there would be no difference between a contract entered into by one contractor and that entered into by another. I expect to get that into shape as soon as the session is over, so that we will have no divergence. It depends now upon the wording of the contract. We found that, in some contracts made with a general clause, we were in a position to insist upon the contractor following the wages even if they went up; in others 1 have been unable to do it.

This question is a very important one, because sometimes workmen are employed believing, that if there should be an increase in wages during the performance of the contract, they are supposed to receive it; and the minister states that the difficulty might be in the wording of the contract. I hope that in future all contracts will be made uniform.
There are sub-contractors who try to evade the law by claiming that they are not the direct contractors. There is a case in point in Montreal, that of the structural ironworkers on the Custom House, about which the minister knows. A rate of only
thirty-five cents an hour was specified in the contract, which was, of course, a mistake; it should have been more. But the sub-contractors state that they are not obliged to pay the fair wage because they are not the general contractors. I understand that this point is not well taken, because when a man signs a contract he is supposed to abide by the specification and the specification always has a fair wage clause attached to it. I ask the hon. minister to be sure that in the future no possible loophole is left in these schedules, so that the men will be put on an equal footing, and will know full well what they are going to receive.
Something has been done in .Montreal, especially on the Lachine canal where an officer sent by the Minister of Labour classified the men to their entire satisfaction. They had not been properly classified, and were not paid the regular wages. They were classified absolutely outside of the work they were performing. But the fair wages officer went there and made an arrangement satisfactory to the men in accordance with the fair-wage clause.
The Minister of Labour can never use too much prudence in so far as these contracts are concerned, because we are liable at any time to have to deal with an unscrupulous contractor or sub-contractor who will try to read between the lines of the contract, and create trouble for the men and for the department. I hope it can be obviated in future, and I am glad my hon. friend is taking steps to see that contracts shall be uniform, so that the men will be in a position to know exactly where they are.

My hon. friend misunderstood me. I have not promised that in all future contracts there will be a clause providing that the contractor shall have to pay higher wages if the wages go up. What I promised was that I w'ould try to have uniformity in that respect in all the contracts. I might tell my hon. friend that we do not recognize the sub-contractor at all; we have nothing to do with the sub-contractor. However, if complaints are made that the schedules prepared by us are not being closely observed, we send out an officer who may see the sub-contractor and try to arrange with him to pay the schedule figure. But when it comes to exerting any pressure we do not deal with the sub-contractor at all. If we can make an amicable arrangement with him we do so; but if we

cannot then we fall back onthe contractor; he is the man that we hold responsible. I give very close attention to that. I know that men sometimes do not complain if they do not get the fair-wage prices, and every case that my attention has been called to I have had investigated. I have often had men paid as much as one hundred dollars for back pay where the contractor kept them below the minimum rate; and when he does not comply with the department's demands, we withhold the amount of money he should receive at the end of the month, or at the end of two months. In a great many cases we have secured back pay for men, and in every case we do our very best to see that the men are paid. I may tell my hon. friend that I have no sympathy whatever with contractors who, speaking generally, make very large profits out of work they do for the Government; and I think there is no excuse whatever for them to squeeze the men to the lowest cent they can get them for. I insist on their paying the highest wage that is provided for by the fair-wage officers.

Does the minister not think that the Harbour Commission of Montreal should pay the current rate of wages paid by ordinary contractors in that city ? Why should the commission pay les3 than the contractors ? The commission argue that their work is not Government work and is under their control. I remember that in 1911 a difficulty concerning wages arose at the port of Montreal, and there was a strike on, in the settlement of which I had something to do; and the wages paid by important contractors in Montreal were the wages the investigating commission decided should he paid to the men. It was after the expiration of the agreement between the Harbour Commission and the carpenters that trouble arose last year. I do not see why the Harbour Commission, who can afford to pay as well as the best contractor in the city, should fall behind the law and not pay fair wages out of the public moneys they handle, in which the Government is directly or indirectly interested. It seems to me that the very highest wages should be paid by those who are in direct or indirect connection with the Government. The trouble that arose last year is past; we cannot settle that; but I suppose the present dispute can be settled. At the same time I would ask the minister to use every endeavour to force the Harbour Commission, if possible, at present and in future to pay the regular

rate of wages, which, at the present time is forty-five cents per hour in Montreal. The minister knows there is now some trouble in Montreal, because last Sunday he sent an officer there, whose instructions are to bring about an agreement of some kind, if possible. But the wages paid by our best contractors should also be paid by this board; and I reiterate my request that the minister apply the fair-wage clause. The men have been misled. I know that the minister, as a lawyer, has given the interpretation of the far-wage clause that I have given. He states now that it might be inserted in such contracts, but, of course, he cannot promise. It seems to me that there should be no difference in contracts whether they are large or small or in what part of the country they may be. If there is an increase of wages in one city during the performance of a contract, if the contract stipulates that such an increase in wages shall be given to the men employed on it, then that same rate should be paid in all cities; it should be uniform as far as possible. It would be unfair to take advantage of a small town or city. A fair-wage clause is a fair-wage clause, it does not matter where it is. I hope the minister will look this up and do the best he can. I do not wish the minister to think I am contending that the fair-wage clause should secure the same price for labour all over the country; I know enough about labour conditions to know that is impossible. But whenever an increase of wages is agreed upon, according to the finding of his officer, the increase should be made to apply all over the country.

I am thankful to my hon. friend for mentioning the case of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners. I have insisted upon their paying the same rate of 'wages that reputable contractors are paying in the same town or city. They are, in effect, spending public moneys and I think the public can afford to pay the workingman and the mechanic as much as other reputable contractors are paying. But my hon. friend is aware that in order to take work like the Montreal harbour and the Qubec harbour and other places out of the direct control of the Government these boards were created by a statute and, in a sense, they are independent of the Government altogether. They were appointed for that very purpose, so that they can carry on these great works in each particular harbour without any interference on the part of politicians or members of the Govern-

ment or any one else. We cannot change that except by statute; but we can use our good offices with them to induce them to pay what we think they ought to pay. We do not see any reason why a harbour commission should not pay a carpenter the same rate of wages as is paid by a contractor across the street, and I have been urging them to do that. They have promised now to consider, with our fair-wage officers, any complaints that may be made and to do what they can to meet the conditions that they may have to contend with. At the present time, without any very satisfactory provisions, we are unable to do anything else. We might use drastic means by dismissing the commission or something of that sort, but we have not gone to such an extent as that and I do not suppose my hon. friend would insist upon any such action.

I would call attention to the appointment of fair-wage officers. I do not know whether the minister has been well advised or not, but I am pretty sure that sometimes fair-wage officers are appointed who know very little about the labour movement. For instance, I believe that last year the minister appointed one in Winnipeg who did not know the leaders of the labour movement there. He was asked if he knew Mr. Riggs, now an aider-man in Winnipeg, who has been identified with the .labour movement there for a great many years, and he said that he had heard of him. The same thing occurred in reference to a number of other prominent labour men. The minister may say it is probably better that the fair-wage officer should not know the labour men; but the minister must agree that if a fair-wage officer wishes to get information from the men's standpoint the only place he can get it in any city is at the labour temple where the labour men gather. For instance Mr. Dubreuil, whom I know and who is one of the best fair-wage officers the minister has-and I know his knowledge and ability as a tradesman because I have worked with him-when he wishes to get information in Montreal he goes to the labour temple. He does the same thing in every other city in the eastern provinces. I hope that in the appointment of fair-wage officers no attention is paid to politics because, of course, the position is absolutely independent of politics. The minister will understand that if a fair-wage officer does not have the confidence, to some extent, of both labour men and em-328
ployers he will not be able to do justice to the department or to either side. The minister cannot expect to have from him as good service as from a man enjoying that confidence. If the minister in appointing fair-wage officers would consult the trades councils of the different cities, I am sure that he would get good men, We all know Mr. Dubreuil. He is a good man. Mr. McNiven is also a good man and a practical man of experience. The late Mr. O'Donohue also rendered great service to the department through his knowledge of the real conditions of labour not only in his own city but throughout the country. It seems to me that in a Labour Department, as far as possible the labour world should be consulted.

I am glad my hon.
friend has brought up the question of the appointment of a fair-wage officer at Winnipeg. When I assumed charge of the department we had only two fair-wage officers for all Canada. He has been in Winnipeg now for six or seven months, and has done a great deal of work



for the department. I am perfectly satisfied that he is doing his work and doing it iwell.	[DOT]

My hon. friend was not present when the hon. member for Pictou asked a similar question, but I do not object to repeating what I said then. My hon. friend will remember that it was proposed by the late Government to ap(-point a commission to inquire into industrial conditions and technical education in Europe and the United States. Realizing that education is one of the matters exclusively assigned to the various legisla-
	-
tures of Canada under the British North America Act, my predecessor communicated with the Prime Ministers of the various provinces asking them severally if they had any objections to the appointment of such a commission. I stated that the only object of the Government was to gather information on these matters and make a report for the benefit of the legislatures. All the Prime Ministers replied to that communication, and none of them made any objections, but the Prime Minister of Ontario and the Prime Minister of Quebec pointed out in their replies that under the British North America Act the legislatures had exclusive jurisdiction over education, and said that if it were distinctly understood that the whole scope of the commission was to gather information and submit it for the benefit of the legislatures they would have no objection, but that they wanted that distinctly understood. As my hon. friend is aware, the commission went beyond that in their recommendations. The report was not ready for distribution until last April, and more particularly the last volume which deals with conditions in Canada. As soon as the report was ready, we sent copies to the various Prime Ministers throughout Canada with the request for an expression of opinion as to these recommendations, and as to the position they would take with reference to them. We have heard from some of the Prime Ministers, but not all. This matter has been under the consideration of the Cabinet, and it was thought wise not to enter upon any definite scheme until we had heard from the various provincial Governments. Personally, I am very much in favour of doing anything in Teason for the extension of technical education and industrial training. I do not anticipate that the provincial Governments will object to getting some money for educational purposes. I think the Parliament of Canada will be willing to materially assist the local legislatures in providing for technical education and industrial training. I regard it as of very great importance to the people of Canada.

I do not suppose that any provincial government would refuse a grant from the federal Parliament for the purposes of technical education and1 industrial training. I am very sorry that the Government has not seen fit to take away from the Militia Estimates the amount I suggested to be used for purposes of technical education in this country.

I am sure that the minister will agree with me in saying that his department is not getting enough. The Labour Department has been relegated to the very last place among the departments ever since it has been formed. This should not be so, because it is a department that has greater demands made upon it every year, and it would have been a splendid thing in the interests of labour and of the country generally if it had been permitted to occupy its proper place in relation to the other departments of Government. We have been allowing this department and its work to go back year after year, when there is a feeling prevalent throughout the country that a certain amount of money should be expended upon the objects for which the department was created. For instance, what are we doing for the organization and maintenance of technical schools for the instruction of men and boys? There are a number of schools of this class already in existence, and they afford opportunities to men and boys to take either night or day courses. In the city of Montreal we will have quite a number of boys coming out from these schools who have taken the full course, and I can assure the minister that he would be surprised at the high degree of technical knowledge and skill which have been acquired by boys of seventeen and eighteen years of age. I have known first-class mechanics, skilled in different kinds of work, to make the confession, upon coming into contact with some of these boys, that the 'boys knew more about their trades than they themselves did. I am sorry that the Government has not seen fit this year to grant an amount of money for the encouragement and assistance of these schools. There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. What does the minister intend to do about the regulation of employment bureaus in the large cities? I believe a demand has been made upon him that some form of regulation should be provided, and I believe also that he has expressed himself in favour of it. The suggestion is that the department should have control of these bureaus, and if it had it would save a great deal of trouble. Notwithstanding the fact that a request has been made for such regulation, I do not see any Bill upon the OrdeT Paper to put it in a legislative form. Such a Bill could be passed in one or two days, because I am sure that nobody would be against anything of the kind.

While we have not
reached the item in regard to industrial training and technical education, I wish to say a few words, in accord with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Murphy) has just said, along the lines of industrial and technical education as far as this Government is concerned. When the Estimates of the Department of Militia and Defence were up the other night I gave my opinion as to what this Government should do for technical education and the reason I did so was that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes) made the statement that more good was being derived from' military training than would be derived from technical education. That was a rather peculiar way of putting it and I took-the opportunity then to take strong ground against any such statement coming from the Minister of Militia. I am sure that the Minister of Labour does not agree with the Minister of Militia in that and I am also convinced that the people of the country do not agree with him. The commission that was appointed by the late Administration made a very voluminous report after having gathered valuable information not only in Canada and the United States but also in European countries. They made a number of recommendations. The minister may have been right in saying that the commissioners had gone outside of their commission in making these recommendations, but I would scarcely think that the commission would have been doing justice to themselves or to the people who appointed them if they had not done so.
I did not say, or I did not intend to say, that they went outside of their commission; I said that they went outside of the communication that was sent to the various provinces.

I understand that the
provinces made some reservations as to the powers that were given to the commission. But, however, they made a recommendation and that recommendation commends itself to industrial Canada and to Canada as a whole. There is nothing in my humble judgment that goes so far in keeping the population which we have within our confines, and also encouraging a good class of immigration from abroad, as an efficient system of technical education. While I agree with the minister that education is within the purview of the local legislatures I want to point out that we have, in item 286, provided for industrial training and technical education, thus showing that

there is really no very great restriction after all upon the Dominion Government in dealing with this matter. The minister is certainly right in saying that the provincial governments from the Atlantic to the Pacific would be very glad to receive a sum of money, such as was recommended by the commission, to be used by the various provinces for technical education. This Parliament has voted, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture, a very large sum of money for the teaching of agriculture in the schools of the various provinces. The scheme is a good one and the Minister of Agriculture has told the House that it is meeting with success.
The same thing can be done in reference to the organization of technical education. I have received from Mr. Hanrahan, the secretary of the Mining Society in Sydney, the same resolution that was sent to my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) praying the Government to take into consideration, at the very earliest moment, the matter of distributing such a sum of money as was recommended by the commission for technical education in the various provinces. I need not again go particularly into the question of all that has been accomplished by technical education in the industrial centres of Canada. I pointed out the other night that in the industrial centres of Nova Scotia, especially in regard to the steel and coal companies, every man holding a permanent position, from the general manager down, had got his promotion through the education which he received in the technical and night schools which were provided in that part of the country by the Nova Scotia Government. The Nova Scotia Government, or any other local government, has a limit to the amount of money that it can spend on technical education, and in a country with a revenue such as Canada has, or in a country that is spending between $14,000,000 and $15,000,000 on military enterprise and development annually, we ought to be able to spend $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 annually in the interest of technical education.
I am very greatly interested in this matter because I represent a constituency where technical education has made more progress, and its results have been more apparent probably, than any other constituency in Canada. I am peculiarly interested, however, in the fact that the people are clamouring for a better system of technical education in that part of the country than that which has hitherto existed. The City Council of Sydney has voted a free site

for a technical school to co-operate, if possible, with the technical school at Halifax. The people of Sydney have also, through their city council, undertaken to contribute a sum towards the upkeep and maintenance of the school. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour probably remembers that he was at the meeting for the organization of the committee that had this work under control, and we were all glad to see him there. He heard some of the discussion and took part in it himself. While he would not probably have been justified in making any definite promise, he told those present that he would bring the matter to the attention of the Government, and I presume he has done so.
If I had the time I would go into the question of technical education to a greater extent, but I will only say that, when we see places in Canada willing to contribute to the upkeep of technical schools, when we *see private citizens going down into their pockets and donating money for technical schools, when we see people who have been trained in these technical schools devoting their extra time and leisure to teaching and tutorship in the night schools, I think it is certainly incumbent upon this Government, with its vast resources and revenue, to do something for technical education. I appeal to the Minister of Labour to use his good influence with the Government to bring this matter to a happy conclusion. I appeal to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), who is a Nova Scotian, and who understands and realizes perhaps better than any other gentleman on the other side of the House what technical education has done for his native province, and I appeal to his Government to give this matter of technical education, and the report and recommendations of the commission, their very best consideration during this summer and not to stop at consideration but to bring forward something tangible at the next session of Parliament and try to help technical education and show the country and the world that we are not interested alone in military manoeuvres, in building armouries and in spending millions upon millions in the effort to develop a military spirit in this country, but that we are also interested in developing a citizenship that will be second to none and which can only be developed in its highest form by a wise and liberal policy in regard to technical education.

Cam the minister say briefly how far negotiations have been completed as between this Government and the British Columbia Government in regard to the Indian reserves?

The British Columbia
Commission were at work during the summer and fall of last year; but they took a protracted holiday during the winter season, and the work was somewhat delayed owing to the fact that the chairman of the commission had resigned. This necessitated the appointment of another chairman; and Mr. White, one of the old commissioners was appointed to that position, another gentleman, Mr. Carmichael, being appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the promotion of Mr. White. The commission have been at work during the past six weeks, and are visiting each reserve and taking evidence. They have covered a goodly portion of the province, iand intend in the immediate future to visit the reserves in the more remote part3 of the province. I do not expect they will have their work completed until well on in the fall. They have not sent in any report as yet, except some emergency items in connection with surrenders and rights of way.
Will final action be taken on their report without reference to legislation by Parliament?

I do not think there will be any final action taken at all. The report will, no doubt, be received prior to the next meeting of Parliament, and, of course, it will require joint action on the part of the province and of-the Dominion. I do not expect that anything definite and final will be passed until Parliament has a chance to discuss the matter.

What I want to get at is: Is the Government acting under legislative authority already given by Parliament that would allow the matter to be closed up without further reference to Parliament, or has a commission been appointed merely to get information upon which parliamentary action will subsequently be based?
I think it was the intention to have Parliament finally pass upon it; I do not think there is any legislation by which we can wind up the matter without submitting it to Parliament.

I want to get whatever
information I can in regard to the attitude of the department towards the Kitsilano reserve, and I would like to have the minister's explanation as to how and why the Government of British Columbia was permitted to deal with these Indians with a view to acquiring property rights in the reserve.

I was not so personally
conversant with this, owing to my absence last session when this question came up, but I understand that the British Columbia Government claim a reversionary right in the property. They negotiated with these Indians without any sanction, so far as I am aware, from this Government, and made certain financial arrangements. All the papers in this matter are before the Royal Commission. It has not been taken up as yet by the commission, I presume, possibly in the hope that some amicable ar. rangement may be arrived at between the two governments. At any rate the deparment does not recognize the action of the British Columbia Government with reference to this reserve, and of course, will not give any title by reason of their negotiations with the Indians. The Indian Department will give no recognition whatever to the action of the British Columbia Government, which cannot receive a title to these lands under their present arrangement without the consent of the department, and, of course, it is not the intention of the department to have the lands disposed of in the manner in which they have been disposed of. As I said before, this is one of the matters, in connection with other reservations, referred to the commission, who will report upon it.

I understand that our officials were net called into requisition at all to get the consent of the Indians. It was done by the officials of the British Columbia Government. I do not think that our officers are at all responsible for whatever action has been taken. The officials may have been conversant with what has been going on; they may have been awaTe that certain arrangements were being made by the British Columbia Government, but under no instructions whatever from headquarters, and it was not with the consent, or under the direction or jurisdiction of our Indian agents there, that any surrender of the property of the Indians was obtained.

I wish to emphasize this point:	That the Government, having
officials on the ground whose duty it was to protect the rights of the Indians, if those rights were not protected it was the fault of the officials, and if the officials have not been punished for that fault, then this Government must accept full responsibility foT the action that was taken.

I wish to bring up a matter that is not exactly relevant to this item. I would like to ask what action the Government is taking upon the petition of the Board of Trade of Anti-gonish with respect to the establishment of an immigration agency?

That is a petition which, I think, has only reached the department within the last few days, and I understand that a deputation is coming to interview the Government about it. No action has been taken as yet, as the matter has not been fully gone into.

I think that the proposed deputation has been called off. I have sufficient confidence in the minister to believe that he will do justice in this matter without having it impressed upon him any further by a deputation. What would be the policy of the Government in that regard? It is claimed that, inasmuch as farms are being depopulated in the eastern part of the country, and as the Government has done a great deal for the West in the matter of encouraging immigration in that section, it is time now that something should be done for the East, and that there should be an immigration agency for the eastern part of the country. The minister might tell me what the policy of his department is in that regard.

The department has devoted more attention to immigration matters in the eastern provinces during the last year or two than has been done in the past. In order to carry out our policy we have appointed officers to act in conjunction with the provincial officers in the Maritime provinces. We have an officer in Nova Scotia, appointed a year or so ago, who is acting for the Dominion Government in placing immigrants going to that province upon the land. I believe also that the provincial Government have officials of their own engaged in similar work; I know they have one in the neighbouring province of New Brunswick. In addition to having these gentlemen in our employ, we are quite willing to adopt the same policy in regard to the Maritime provinces that we have with regard to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; that is, we have in certain counties, or a group of counties, officers who are paid a commission on every adult farmer or labourer whom they place with farmers upon the land. We are quite willing to extend that system if it is considered desirable by the people of the Maritime provinces.
What we are asking for down there is a sum of 810,000, to open an immigration bureau or agency. We estimated that it would cost that.
We have not an item in the Estimates to bear the expense of opening up any immigration agency.
That has not been your policy in the past?
No, it has not.

So far as encouraging immigration in the eastern part of the country is concerned, I do not think that this Government can claim any greater credit than its predecessor. The only attempt at encouraging immigration there was the appointment of some agents to go to the old country. I think there were seven or eight from Nova Scotia who were sent over last year at an expense of something between $700 to $900. I had the opportunity of reading over the reports, and in most cases there is no doubt but that these men were sent for the purpose of giving them a trip; they were faithful friends and had to be given a little recreation, and they got three months' vacation at the country's expense. I read one of the reports, and the only information given is that the man visited the Highlands and found the people very hospitable. That is information that could have been found out at home. This man also stated that he had met lots of people with whom he had conversed in the vernacular, and with whom he had spoken in the language of the Garden of Eden. As a matter of fact, most of the agents were men who could not tell the boundaries of the Dominion of Canada, or who is Governor General; or how Canada is governed. And yet they were sent over, spent time and money over there, came home and got somebody to write the report for them.

On the general question of immigration, while I do not wish to delay the House, I want to say that I do not think, so far as we have heard yet, the Government appreciates the situation that is abroad in the country to-day in regard to employment, and in regard to the prospect of employment during the coming winter. It goes without saying that with the practical completion of two enormous railway enterprises there must result a tremendous readjustment of labour conditions. This is the fact as we have it, coupled with the cessation of that expansion and prosperity that we have had in past years. The situation at the present time is unfortunate, if not alarming, and we are only at the beginning of the season. I fear to contemplate what the condition is likely to

be at the coming on of winter unless there is a business revival that is not at the moment in prospect. While this is the condition it seems to me that it would be the part of wisdom for the Government to recognize that condition and enforce an effective embargo (upon labour immigration. My hon. friend has said that he is enforcing now the regulations that prevailed in 1907 under similar conditions, when the emigrating populations of other countries were warned that Canada only needed farm labourers and domestic servants. I am afraid that we are beyond the point when a mere announcement of that kind will be sufficient, and that to-day our position is such that we should only admit people who have money enough to go on the land. I do not see any necessity of declaring a permanent exclusion policy, but under the exceptional conditions now prevailing, and with the prospects that are before us, I am counselling the Government in all good faith and without any desire to criticise unduly, that, in my judgment, it would be the part of wisdom at the present time to put an embargo on the coming to Canada of any people who are not in a position to support themselves at any rate for a year, or who are not coming to conditions that would ensure their support for a year. I would strongly urge the Government to recognize the conditions as they are and the prospects that are before us and to deal with them in a drastic manner. I do not think that it is good policy to let things drift. Considering the situation as it was last fall and this spring, and the prospect of the situation next fall, this is the time for drastic and energetic action on the part of the Government.

I realize the seriousness of khe .situation, as pointed out by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), although 'I do not take as gloomy an outlook as he does. I have done the utmost in my power to impress upon steamship agents and Government officials to discourage emigrants from coming to Canada unless they are coming to assured employment, or unless they are domestic servants or agricultural labourers. The very best evidence that our efforts in that respect are meeting with, success is, that immigration to Canada has fallen off more than fifty per cent this year. The most of those now coming to Canada are coming with the intention of going on the land. I do not think it would give our country a very enviable reputation to absolutely exclude all labourers from all

parts of Canada at present. We are enforcing more strictly this year than ever before the provision in regard to the money qualification which was fixed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) himself when Minister of the Interior. Our immigration agents have been made acquainted with the condition of affairs in this country; they have received their instructions, and I think they are carrying them out to the letter. I join with the hon. gentleman in hoping that the financial situation may so improve with the good crop we expect this year, that there will not in future be any complaint about unemployment. Most of our immigrants, who come to engage in other than agricultural and domestic employment, come on the invitation of friends who supply them with the money, or else they have money of their own.

It was stated in the newspapers that in the week of June 5, 3,500 immigrants had arrived at Quebec. 1 would be glad if all those would go on the land or are coming to assured employment, but I very much doubt it. We hope there Will be a good crop, and that conditions will be better in the fall, tot now is the time to make provision for unfavourable conditions. With the cessation of great railway works, there are necessarily .a large number of men thrown out of employment who must find work somewhere else.

This question of Hindu immigration has reached an acute stage in Canada. Has the Prime Minister been in communication with the Imperial authorities, so as to bring this matter before a future Imperial conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have had no information yet with regard to any approaching Imperial conference and therefore the subject which the hon. gentleman alludes to has not been under consideration. When an Imperial conference is called, the various governments will be requested to put forward subjects for discussion and these will constitute the agenda. It would be impossible to say at this moment whether or not this subject would be discussed but one would naturally suppose that in the ordinary course of events it would come up for consideration.

When we were discussing the Hindu situation a few days ago, I stated that the newspapers had reported that the Ghinese were being admitted, while the Hindus were being held up, notwithstanding the exclusion order. The minister then said that this was not the case. I presume the minister has made further inquiry, and I would be glad if he would make another statement as to whether or not that is actually the fact.

A large proportion of these Chinese who came in the vessel referred to by the newspapers was in bond going to the West Indies; another proportion was returning to Canada, having previous domicile here. There were quite a few of them who were coming to Canada for the first time, but by reason of the fact that the required thirty days' notice had to be given before enforcing the provisions of the Order in Council against the Chinese and. the original Order in Council not having been enforced against them, these were allowed in. Since that vessel's arrival, all
Chinese of the labouring class will have the Order in Council enforced against them, the same as it is against the Hindus.

At some risk I wish to
give expression to my views in regard to the immigration of Chinese. I think the figures will bear me out that in the estimation of every well-wisher of Canada there are more Chinese coming to Canada at the present time and under present conditions than is good for Canada. The mere fact that we levy a toll upon those who come does not in any degree better the conditions resulting from their coming. They are here, and they are coming in increasing numbers notwithstanding the payment of this head tax, and my individual opinion is that a condition has arrived that calls for some new arrangement that will adequately prevent the coming of Chinese to Canada in such numbers as at present. I consider that the numbers in which they are coming now constitute a menace to the well-being of the country. It is of such large dimensions as to tend to actually shift the basis of civilization in our most western province. I make this announcement with the view of urging the Government to adopt some policy that shall be effective in measurably excluding that immigration. When the $500 head tax was first put on it was effective for a short time, and when it ceased to be effective it was hoped that there was only a temporary abnormal rush of immigration. But time has demonstrated that the Chinese have adjusted themselves to the conditions of the head tax and that while the Government of British Columbia and of Canada are levying much revenue on the Chinese, the standard of Canadian civilization is being seriously affected by the large and increasing numbers of Chinese who are coming into Canada.
