Is it the intention of the Government to purchase the necessary land as a site for a public building in Wotton?
We have had an application but I have not been able to give it consideration up to the present time. I hope to do so after the close of the session.

I wish to call attention to a case which has come under my observation in connection with a former employee of the Public Works Department, Mr. B. J. Franklin. I understand that Mr. Franklin
was a messenger in the House of Commons during last session and that sometime after the session was over he was placed in the Department of Public Works as a clerk with technical knowledge of plans and specifications, etc, and that therefore it was not necessary, he having been recommended, to have him pass a civil service examination. I have here a memorandum to the chief architect by Mr. R. C. Wright, the assistant architect, recommending Mr. Franklin, and a memorandum to the deputy minister by the chief architect endorsing that recommendation. These memorandums are as follows:
July 15, 1913.
Memorandum to the Chief Architect.
I have much pleasure in recommending Mr. B. J. Franklin to a clerical position in this branch. We have been cataloging all the plans for the Architectural Department, and have found his assistance very valuable.
As the number of new buildings increases, the task of retaining control in making out lists for blue prints, receiving and numbering of the drawings, forwarding specifications for printing and to contractors, and to many other details of filing, require more than one person and Mr. Franklin, with his knowledge of plans will make a first-class addition.
R. C. Wright,
Asst. Chief Architect.
Ottawa, July 15, 1913.
Memorandum to the Deputy Minister.
Attached is a memo, from Mr. Wright, my assistant, recommending the appointment of Mr. B. J. Franklin to a clerical position in this branch. I concur with Mr. Wright's recommendation.
D. Ewart, Chief Architect.
On the strength of those letters, I understand, Mr. Franklin was given a clerkship in the department at $75 a month or $800 a year. After he had been there, and paid at this rate, for some time, some 'question arose between the Department and the Civil Service Commission as to Mr. Franklin passing an examination. I understand that the Civil Service Commission gave him a certificate as a messenger but that he had never asked for such a certificate and was not hired as a messenger nor was he doing messenger's work. I have a letter from the Deputy Minister of Public Works to the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission:
9th October, 1913.
Sir,-Will you kindly let me have a reply to my letter of July 17 last, enclosing this department's file No. 6174, with reference to the temporary employment of Mr. B. J. Franklin as a

clerk in subdivision ' B ' of the second division, at $800 per annum.
I am, Sir,
Tour obedient servant,
(Signed) J. B. H., Deputy Minister.
The Secretary,
Civil Service Commission,
Ottawa.
If this man was hired on the ground that he had technical knowledge, and so complied with the Act, it would seem most unfair for the department to have afterwards paid him off as messenger. I understand that he received for his services $250, and is claiming a balance of $200, a total of $450.

I have no knowledge of
the case, but I am informed that when Mr. Franklin was taken on it was in the hope that he would serve as a technical officer in the architects' branch. When he went up for examination before the Civil Service Commission they would not pass him for any position other than that of a messenger, and as we had no position for a messenger we could not retain him. That accounts for his position.

Are persons not taken
into the Civil Service without certificates from the commission on the ground that they have technical knowledge of the work which they are required to do?
The Civil Service Commission makes an examination and certifies that the candidate is qualified.
Then I think the fault must lie with the Civil Service Commission because this man had the letters which I have read showing that he had the technical qualifications necessary.
I am not acquainted with all the facts, but I shall have the case looked up.
If there is any merit in the case the minister might pay the balance this man is asking.

An amount has been in
the Estimates for some two years for the construction of an addition to the public building in Chatham, N.B. It had been expected by the residents of the town that this building would have been constructed last year. The money has been voted. Will the work go on during the present season?

It is true there has been some delay in connection with this work by reason of the fact that, as we sometimes

do, we had engaged an outside architect to prepare the plans for the addition to the building at Chatham. I understand that the matter has now been righted and the work will proceed as soon as possible.

There is some force in the remarks of my hon. friend in this respect, at all events, that the present Government have been raither ambitious in the buildings they have erected, and the same probably is true of our predecessors. This has been recognized by members on both .sides of the House during the last two or three years. As my hon. friend says, if we are going to provide public buildings throughout the country, we shall have to erect them at a more moderate cost than formerly, because it would be impossible for us to erect public buildings in all the towns and villages applying for them at the price we have been paying in the past. The department has had this matter under consideration, and has given instructions to the architects that in future more attention must be paid to the size and cost of the public buildings to be erected. In a town with a population of 1,000 or 1,500 people, I think a satisfactory building could be erected for $10,000 or $12,000 ait the most. We wish to give public buildings to the different places that really need them, and in future we are going to pay more attention to the size and cost of buildings erected.
I entirely agree with my hon. friend's policy. To spend $20,000 for a post office that has a revenue of only $1,300 seems to me absurd.

What I am going to say will no doubt be combatted by my hon. friend from North Renfrew. I need not go into too many details, as we have both brought up this matter before in the House. In my judgment, the Government has done a great wrong in changing the location of a post office from the south riding of Renfrew to the north riding. The village of Eganville is noted, amongst other things, foT being the birthplace of many great men.
Born on the north side of the river.

The north side should not have the great men and the post office too. The village of Eganville is divided by the river Bonnechere and a part of the village is in South Renfrew and a part in North Renfrew. For half a century the post office has been in the south riding. Some years ago it was quite a distance from the river, but owing to certain representations made by the late Mr. Mackie, then member for North Renfrew, the post office was removed down to practically the end of the bridge on the south side so as to be easier of access for the people of the village and particularly those on the north side. A fire swept the village some years ago and it became necessary to have a new post office. At that time it was recognized that the post office had always been in the south riding, and Mr. Low, who was the member for the south riding, was instrumental in having the ex-Minister of Public Works put an item in the Estimates for a public building in that village. The item was put in, but owing to certain disastrous circumstances for the country, a change took place in 1911 and the vote was not expended. Later in 1911 there was a strong agitation on the north side as well as the south side, each side wanting the new post office. I do not think I need read the correspondence. The hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. White) represented strongly the claims of that side, and representations were made strongly for the south side. There were petitions put in from both sides of the river, and representations were made by my hon. friend and by others to whom I shall refer in a moment. In 1912, when a by-election was going on, managed by the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), the Department of Public Works got very busy, and I find that there was a report made by Mr. Hunter in 1912. That was right in the middle of the election, but the report was made so that it would not hurt the north side or help the south side. It was very vague; in fact, Mr. Hunter did not commit himself. He said in the conclusion of the report:
I would especially point out that I am report-ting on two separate properties, without making any recommendation in favour of one or the other leaving it to your judgment or that of the head, or deputy head of the department, to make the recommendation to the Government for its approval.

The property on the north side was known as the Bonfield property and that on the south as the Mills property. The election took place in February and, in March, the Bonfield property was bought on the north t side just after the election, was over notwithstanding the fact that it had been suggested that the property on the south side was likely to be bought. In fact I do not think that a great many people thought that the post office would likely be changed. After the election, resulting in favour of the Liberal candidate, the property was immediately bought on the north side.
Is it not a fact that the Government had never owned a post office building in Eganville?

I did not mean to insinuate that they did. Up to that time the post office had been in a rented building. This was the first time that a public building was to be erected. That property was bought in March right after the election. I asked the Minister of Public Works last session when the Estimates were going through about these properties and he told me that there were properties on both sides of the river under consideration. In that, I think he must have been mistaken because the property was already bought on the north side. Strong representations were made by men representing both sides of the river. I wish to point out in fairness to the gentleman who was my opponent at that time that he wrote several letters to the department urging strongly the location on the south side of the river where the post office had always been. The reeve of the village also urged the Government to retain the post office on the south side. In addition to that the village council unanimously passed a resolution asking that it be left on the south side. A strong letter was written by Rev. Father Dowdall, a resident of twenty years standing and a man well known and greatly beloved all through that county asking that it be lleft on the south side.
I want to protest as strongly as I can against the action of the Government. My hon. friend (Mr. Rogers) who is now the Minister of Public Works was not then Minister of Public Works but the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) was the same (Postmaster General we have now and I think he should have said something as to the location of this post office. I am going to give the reasons which have come to me, and which are within my knowledge, why I make this, possibly the last

protest, against the change in the site of the post office. There is no doubt in my mind that, following very close upon the by-election, it was dangled during the election before the people and the people of the south riding never thought during the by-election that their post office was going to be taken away from them and put on the north side. It was quite a factor in the campaign. My opponent legitimately used it and as a result he received the largest vote that any man had ever received from the people who get their mail from that post office. Everybody will admit that he received twice as many votes as there were Conservative votes there. It was cruel of the Government to punish the people of Renfrew, both Liberal and Conservative, who were induced by that consideration to vote for their candidate. I am going to read the resolution of the council of Eganville and it is not unreasonable to think that the council would have as good an idea as any person could have as to the location of the post office keeping in mind that the post office had always been on the south side of the river.
It was moved by Councillor J. W. Gallagher, and seconded by Councillor J. McNamara, that a resolution be passed and forwarded to the Minister of Public Works at Ottawa recommending the property known as the Bonfield property, part of College Green on the south side of the BonnechSre river, as a site for the post office. Carried unanimously.
At what date was that passed?

July 22, 1912:
I hereby certify that the above is a true copy of a motion passed in council at the village of Eganville, July twenty-second, nineteen hundred and twelve.
Full council present composed of Reeve J. T. McCann, and Councillors J. W. Gallagher, M. D. O'Rielly, H. M. Foy and John McNamara.
Hugh Costello, Clerk, Village of Eganville.
My hon. friend will see that the purchase of the lot was kept very quiet. Even I was told in the House during the session that they were considering the purchase of lots on both sides of the river at that time. I have no doubt that the hon. member for North Renfrew knew that the lot had been purchased a few days after the election was over. I have a memorandum which I believe was forwarded to the Government in which there is some information. The memorandum reads as follows:
In behalf of the signatures of a petition to the Hon. Postmaster General and handed to the Hon. Mr. Monk, Minister of Public Works, re site of new post office at Eganville of which

petition acknowledgment was made to me to the effect that the matter was now in the hands of the Justice Department. I beg to submit the following statements, which, to the best of my belief I declare to be substantially correct:
1.	The BonnechSre river divides the village of Eganville into north and a south side. For federal purposes the north side is in the north riding of Renfrew, and the south side in the south riding of Renfrew.
2.	The post office has been since the beginning of the village, 50 odd years ago, on the south side.
3.	Some 10 years ago as the result of an agitation supported by the late Thomas Mackie, M.P., of North Renfrew, the site was changed from the southern section of the south side to the banks of the BonnechOre, close to the bridge connecting the north and south sides.
4.	The location in which is the Bonfleld property is the most central in the village and it was acceptable then to all.
5.	The initial grant of $2,000 for the new post office was given by the late Liberal Government at the request of Mr. Low, the member for the south riding.
6.	It was not at that time contemplated to change the site.
7.	Since the advent to power of the Conservative Government proposals have been made by the member for North Renfrew to have the site changed to the north side.
8.	The site proposed on the north side is not central, neither is it suitable for a post office, as it is dug into a hill 50 or 60 feet high, and subject to freshets.
9.	The petition for such site is not signed nor favoured by the majority of the business men of the village.
10.	Neither does this site meet the approval of the majority of the village or of the persons receiving their mail at the post office.
11.	On the contrary the great bulk of the business men and of others interested in the site, favour the south side site, near the bridge central, commanding and in every way suitable. -
12.	The south side of the village and the section of the south riding served by the post office have not done anything against the Government to merit a change of site so detrimental to them as the one proposed.
13.	There is ever a means to right this matter even if the north site has been chosen and purchased.
14.	Public agitation has been advisedly kept down to the present in order that the Government after the reconsideration of facts might settle this matter quietly and equitably.
15.	The annexed statistical schedules are respectfully submitted.
The above copy has no name attached to it, hut it was evidently sent because it is among the papers. I have an idea it was prepared by the Rev. Father Dowdall, but I would not say that definitely because I do not know. I will not weary the House this very warm day by going into all the details, but I may point out that on the north side of the river there are eighteen business places, while on the south side, where the post office has always been, there are forty-three. I have here a list of the 329
business firms on each side. There is also this statement:
In checking the names on the voters lists 1911 for north side of the village of Eganville, and Wilberforce, and North Algoma, on the one hand, and for south side of village of Eganville and Gratton on the other hand, the only municipalities, the whole or portions of which receive their mail at Eganville post office, the results show; Eganville, north side, 106. Wilberforce and North Algoma, 134, total 204, Eganville, south *side, 165. Gratton, 213, total 378.
I need not go into the votes cast at the different Dominion elections and the Conservative and Liberal majorities given respectively by the north side or the south side, but I may state that the people on the south side, knowing negotiations were going on for the purchase of a lot on the south side, and never dreaming that the post office was going to be moved to the north side, voted for my opponent by the score irrespective of politics, and certainly from a political standpoint it was a mistake that advice of the Minister of Customs, or the Minister of Railways, whichever is to blame for it, should have been taken to change the post office. The figures as to the people of the surrounding country who get their mail at the post office on the north side and on the south side, is preponderatingly in favour of the south side. According to the statement of Mr. John George, the assessor, the population of the south side of the Bonnechfere is 582, and the population of the north side is 444.
According to the last census returns, page 88, Eganville in North Renfrew had a population of 618 and Eganville in South Renfrew had a population of 571.
These figures have been given to me by the assessor who took the estimate very carefully and his report is dated April 23, 1913, which is two years more recent than the census figures.

According to that the
town is getting smaller.

I am sorry to say that a good many of the smaller places in Ontario are losing population. I have placed this matter before the Government as strongly as I could. It is unfair to remove the post office to the north side; it has raised ill-feeling in Eganville. The site which would have, been selected on the south side was near the bridge, convenient to the great majority of the people, convenient to the great majority of the business places, and



more convenient in every way than the present site. This removal of the post office in a small community from one riding into another has placed those in the Government responsible for it in an unfavourable {light before the people of the south riding and they have come to the conclusion that in a moment of chagrin at a defeat which everybody knew was sure to come to them, they took this post office- from the south riding and transferred it to the north riding of Renfrew. I dlo not Iblame my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. White) for urging it because he is on the north side, but I do blame the eastern Ontario ministers who are responsible for allowing that to be done. These acts of retribution perpetrated by a 'Government are calculated to raise ill-feeling, and a great big political party cannot afford to do that sort of thing. I again protest to the Government and I say that this building ought not to be erected on the north side. I say that in justice to the majority of the people who get their mail at this post office it ought to be erected on the south side of the Bonne-ohfere river near the bridge, so as to be convenient to the great majority of the inhabitants.

I am sorry I did
not happen to be present last session when my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) brought up the question of the site for the Eganville post office, because I wanted an opportunity of showing the House and to the country what in my opinion is a just reason for the action of the Government in purchasing a site on the north side of the river. I have here a return moved for by my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) with respect to the Eganville post office and on page 3,1 find a letter addressed to myself, enclosing a petition. This petition is dated September 25,1911, four days after the memorable 21st of September of that year. It is signed by some seventy odd residents of the town of Eganville, and also, I think, by the reeve of the township of Wilber-force. This petition, as I stated, was forwarded to me with the request that I take up the matter of the purchase of a site for a public building at Eganville and recommending the purchase of the Mills property at a price of $2,000. On receipt of this petition I made a special trip to Ottawa and took the matter up, after the Government was formed, with the Minister of Public Works at that time, the late Hon. Mr. Monk. I endeavoured to point out to Mr. Monk reasons which I thought were

sufficient for the construction of this building on the north side of the river. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) says he does not blame me in the matter. I think that the Government, in view of the representations which have beeen made to them, were perfectly justified in putting the building where they placed it.
My hon. friend referred to the fact that the result of the by-election in South Renfrew had something to do with influencing the Government in deciding on the location of this building. He also pointed out the fact that the lot was purchased in March, 1912, a few weeks after the by-election. If my hon. friend from South Renfrew did not know that the lot had been purchased at that time, I can tell him that a good many of his constituents knew about it. The following letter was sent me from the secretary of the Public Works Department under date of March 19, 1912:
Gerald V. White, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-With reference to your recommendation of the 26th February last relative to the purchase of the site for the Eganville public building, I beg to inform you that an Order in Council has been passed authorizing the department to buy the property of Mr. Alex. Mills, for $2,000. Steps will be taken through the Department of Justice to complete the transaction.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) R. C. Desrochers,
Secretary.
Among the papers brought down at my request is a letter from my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew dated the 26th of March, 1912, a week after I had received this notification that the lot had been purchased, recommending to the then Minister of Public Works, Mr. Monk, the purchase of a site on the south side of the river. When Mr. Hunter, who looks after the selection of sites for the Public Works Department, visited Eganville, he took into consideration both sites; that is, the Mills site on the north side of the river and the Bonfield on the south side of the river. In looking over Mr. Hunter's letter, I find that Mr. Mills gave an option to the Government for a price of $2,000 on his property, some 6,250 square feet in area. Catherine Bonfield gave an option to the Government for the Bonfield property on the south side of the river for a price of $2,350. It is noted in this return that this price is regarded as rather high, and $2,000

is mentioned as a fair and reasonable price. Taking the assessment returns, I find that the Mills property was assessed for $2,400 and the Bonfield property for $2,100, notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Mills accepted $2,000 for his property and Mrs. Bonfield asked $2,350 for her's.

The department could
have expropriated whatever property they desired.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend also referred to some of the reasons why this building should be placed on' the south side of the river, and he said that for the last fifty odd years the post office had been located on the south side. If that i3 a reason, it ought to be a good reason for moving the site to the north side of the river, because I think it has been on the south side long enough. My hon. friend referred to the fact that the Bonfield property was the one which the residents on the south side of the river had in view. When the exmember for 'South Renfrew (Mr. Low) succeeded in getting the late Government to place an appropriation of some $2,000 in the Estimates prior to the last general election, I understand that Mr. Low recommended a site called the McCann site which is not by any means a central one. If the ex-member for South Renfrew had been a little more urgent in the matter, possibly he could have had the McCann site purchased prior to the election.
My hon. friend also referred to a resolution passed by the village council of Egan-ville, which claimed to be a unanimous one calling upon the Government to purchase a site on the south side of the river for this post office. The hon. gentleman did not tell the House, however, that there were some rather peculiar circumstances in connection with that particular resolution. It seems that there had been some friction in the village council in Eganville over some local matter, the nature of which I do not just at present recall. I think a bylaw was voted on, which the town reeve, Mr. Reinke, and several of the councillors on the north side of the river were anxious to see pass. This particular bylaw was defeated by the ratepayers of Eganville, the result being that Mr. Reinke and all the members of the council from the north side >
of the river, with the exception of Mr. Foy, " resigned.
. The result was that the vacancies were 329*
filled by a reeve named Mr. McCann from the south side of the river, leaving only one councillor from the north side of the river in the village council. I have it on pretty good authority that this resolution had been drafted some months prior to its being passed by the village council, and soon as this new council was inaugurated action was taken to pass this resolution and it was claimed that it passed unanimously. I understand that Mr. Foy from the other side, refrained from voting, so that it was not really a unanimous resolution in so far as the council was concerned.
With regard to the population of Eganville, I find on page 88 of the census of 1911 the following:
Eganville, part North Renfrew; population. 618.
Eganville, part South Renfrew: population, 571.
This shows a larger population on the north side than on the south side. Taking the previous census of 1901, I find the following :
Eganville, part North Renfrew: population, 539.
Eganville, part South Renfrew: population, 568.
In other words, in 1901 the village of Eganville had a larger population on the south side than on the north side, whereas in 1911 it had a larger population on the north side than on the south side; and this goes to show that the increase in population in ten years on the north side was seventy-nine compared with an increase during a similar period on the south side of only three.
My hon. friend also refers to the fact that there had been a very disastrous fire in the village of Eganville on, I think, the 9th of July, 1911. That fire started on the south side of the river, but the prevailing wind being a south wind, blew towards the north side, with the result that the north side suffered very much more than did the south side. Naturally, a number of the residents of the north side who were rendered homeless had to obtain temporary places of abode, and a number of them went over to the south side temporarily, which, no doubt, is the reason for the increase of population, according to the figures which my hon. friend gave, on the south side as compared with the figures taken at the time of the census.
I do not wish to detain the House any further, but I simply want to make my position clear with regard to this matter.

I took the ground that from every viewpoint the north side of the river was the proper side on which to have this public building constructed. It is only a matter of not more than 100 or 150 yards between the two sites. To my mind, if the whole village of Eganville had been in either one riding or the other there would have been no dissatisfaction whatever.
There would not have been any desire to move it, either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know about that. But I am free to admit that, in so far as the action of the Government is concerned in this matter, they have done what, to my mind, is in the best interest of the village as a whole, and I am prepared to defend my action and the action of the Government either in this House or in the country.
Dredging, ?3,420,300.

I want to ask the Minister of Public Works with regard to dredging at St. John, and perhaps this is an opportune time to do it. When I was minister I let a contract for dredging on the western side of the harbour, and there was an estimated quantity of dredging to be done. I remember that the work was not commenced just at that part of the harbour where it was first intended to begin; it was commenced further up. After the dredging had gone on for a considerable period I remember that the officials of the department called my attention to the fact that the quantity which had been named in the specifications was about reached, or perhaps, a little bit more than reached, and that it was a grave question as to whether anything more should be done without calling for new tenders. I allowed the work to go on for a short period; there was some work which seemed to me to be quite urgent. But I understand that since the change of government the same company -or it may be a company with another name; yes, it is a company under another name to whom the original work was transferred-have been allowed to continue and have done vast quantities of work, far beyond the quantity which was specified in the original tenders and which was shown on the plan under which those tenders were invited. I would like to ask the hon. minister as to that.

In answer to my hon.
friend, I think the contract to which he refers was to last five years, and to cover a certain area and to do the dredging necessary within the limits of that area, and, as
I Mr. G. V. White.]
I understand it, the work has not yet been completed. The contract only lapses on the 9th of August of this year, and all the work necessary in the area prescribed by that contract has not even yet been completed.

My hon. friend the minister is wrong as to that. While there was a period of years given to complete the contract, the tenders were called for upon certain specifications and certain plans, and there was an estimated quantity of dredging to be done. I am satisfied that that quantity has been exceeded, I think it has been more than doubled since this Government came into power.

From the information
which the chief engineer gives me, I do not think that my hon. friend is correct. Of course, I shall be glad to have the matter looked into to see whether what he says is so or not. But my understanding is that the contract provided that the area to be covered, as well as the depth of the dredging, was to extend over a period of five years, which will expire on the 9th of August next.
As I understand the contract, the area over which they were working, and the depth to which it was to be dredged, have not yet been completed even in accordance with their contract.

I do not want to be hypeortechnical about it, if my hon. friend has given attention to it. I think the contract as originally let was at a reasonable price. The only question would be whether or not, under the law, new tenders should be called for. I do not urge the matter unduly. What was done with regard to the removal of the beacon? I understand that was by a separate contract.
I will get the information for my hon. friend to-morrow.

The erection of a public building in Canning, Nova' Scotia, was mentioned a few weeks ago. Since then the papers have been brought down, and are now in the possession of the House. It appears by the papers that the Government has decided to erect a public building in Canning, and there is a question as to the selection of a site. The late member for the county, Sir Frederick Borden, as I understand, has offered a free site to -the department, which is in a suitable place in the town, but the department does not seem inclined to accept it. They have been negotiating with a gentleman named N. W.

Eaton for a site in another part of the town. The papers show that the department have offered Mr. EaJton $2,000 for a eite, which appears to be uneuited to the erection of a pnlblic building for several reasons. One reason is that it has not sufficient depth. The information I have is that the depth of the site offered by Mr. Eaton, from the street to the rear of the lot, is only 374 feet. Mr. Eaton is professing to sell a site with a depth of 50 feet, hut he only owns 374 feet, as the papers disclose that a search made in the records of the county show that there is a road at the rear next the river, and in order to get the depth of 50 feet he would have to sell to the 'Government a certain part of the road, which he has not power to sell. If the Eaton site is selected, it appears also by the return that the Government will require a certain strip of another piece of land adjoining the 'EaJton lot, owned by a company of which Sir Frederick Borden is the chief stockholder. The Government are proposing to expropriate part of this lot owned by :SiT Frederick Borden's company, in order to join it with the Eaton property to make a site for the building, and they have offered $1,100 for that small strip of land in OTder to make the Eaton property large enough for the building. Sir Frederick Borden's company have refused to accept $1,100, on the ground that the property is not worth $lyl00 or anything like that sum, that it was purchased for a very much smaller sum a few years ago. The company are contesting the case on the ground that the Government are trying to push upon them too much money for this strip of land adjoining the Eaton lot. I understand the case is now before the courts. This is a very unusual state of affairs, but it appers to be a fact, and the question is why are the Government offering $1,100 for a small lot of land which they could purchase for perhaps two or three hundred dollars. The explanation is that Eaton's lot adjoins it, and the department seems to be anxious to pay Eaton $2,000 for his lot, and if they do so they would require to pay Sir Frederick's company $1,100 for the small piece adjoining, in order, as they say, to take the curse off the price of the Eaton property. For this reason, and this reason alone, the $1,100 is being pushed on the owner of the small adjoining lot. In the face of these facts I think the minister should give some explanation. The correspondence is very long, and I
shall not read it. It discloses that Sir Frederick has agreed to give a. free site for the public building, and the site that he offers appears to be well situated and to be acceptable to the inhabitants of the town of Canning. A public meeting was called some time ago, and a petition was drawn up and signed by the people of Canning, addressed to the Minister of Public Works, dated the 16th of February of the present year. It reads as follows:
The undersigned citizens of Canning and vicinity being extremely anxious as to the securing of the best site for the public building about to be constructed here, venture respectfully to communicate their views to the minister.
In so doing they point out that the matter has been carefully considered by the citizens at several public meetings called for the purpose, and that reports of the proceedings of said meetings were duly communicated on September 4 and 13 and October 1, respectively, to the minister and acknowledged by him.
No action having been taken on the resolutions and recommendations thus laid before the Department of Public Works, the undersigned consider it their duty without further delay to urge by this largely signed communication, such immediate action as will bring about the loea-' tion of the building upon a site where it will best serve the convenience of the public, and at the same time prove to be an ornament to the town and a source of pride to its citizens.
The undersigned are aware that such a site is available, the same having been most favourably reported upon by a committee of citizens whose report was unanimously adopted at a largely attended public meeting.
The site in question is situated in the centre of the business part of the town as well, as of the whole community upon commanding ground, in front of the monument, at the mouth of North avenue leading by the railway station and nearly opposite the Waverly hotel. It has a frontage of over one hundred and thirty feet on the south side of Main street, with a corresponding frontage on a public road twenty-one feet wide along the river bank and wharfs running parallel with Main street, having a depth of over sixty feet between the two streets, and affording excellent warehousing facilities.
The undersigned are credibly informed that this site was offered as a free gift to the town of Canning for this purpose as fully set forth in a letter to the Minister of Public Works dated October 1, 1913, signed by the chairman and secretary to the citizens' meeting held at Canning September 23, 1913. The undersigned have good reason for believing that this offer still remains in force, and are sure that the adoption of this site will meet with the approval of the whole community, as being beyond all question the best.
To this statement witness our signature.
Signed by 88 of the electors of Canning.
This petition is signed by no less than 88 of the electors of Canning, comprising men of both political parties, and is now, in the hands of the minister. In order that

Will that affect the
price of the other lot?

That will depend. As I
understand it, we wanted to purchase this particular lot, but the owners refused to sell.	i'
Would it not have been better to expropriate both lots?

Then we undertook to expropriate it. We were able to come to an agreement as regards the other lot at the price fixed upon by Mr. Dawson, the valuator of the department. He is very careful in making estimates of this character, and his work along this line has been very satisfactory to the department. I have every confidence in him and feel sure that any recommendation made by him will be justified by the facts. We have selected the site he recommended, deeming it to be in the public interest.

Will the Minister of
Public Works be kind enough to say whether he proposes to erect the fence around the public buildings at Antigonish? Several years ago, after the new building was put up there, the concrete foundation for an iron fence was built and there was a vote of $500 in the Estimates of 1912 to put the iron railing around the lot. But that item disappeared and nothing has been done since. I understand that the reason why this was not proceeded with in 1912 was that there was a difficulty about the foreman, or the man who should expend this little item. If the minister has any anxiety about it I will recommend a man myself. The lot is rather unsightly as a result of not putting up this fence. Architect Hewitt prepared the design of the fence, Mr. Ewart, the chief architect, approved of it and the money was put in the Estimates but has disappeared.

I have no knowledge of the circumstances to which my hon. friend refers and my deputy does not appear to have any recollection of it either, but we have taken a note and we will take the matter up with the chief architect.

I would also like to ask the minister if he has acted on the resolution that was passed by the Board of Trade of Antigonish asking for the dredging of Antigonish harbour. There was a resolution passed to the following effect:
Resolved that the federal Government he asked to instruct the local Department of Public Works to prepare an estimate of the cost of opening the present entrance to the Antigonish harbour by deepening the channel across the bar, and further, to instruct said department to ascertain the cost of straightening the harbour channel from No. ll's point (so called) to the present wharf; and further, the cost of deepening channel from the present wharf to Salmon Hole; and further, that when plans and estimates thereof are prepared by said department the Government be asked to vote a sum sufficient for the performance of said work.
The board of trade was a little in error, because, as a matter of fact, the department had been asked a few years ago to have this attended to and a survey was made. It would not therefore be necessary for the local representatives of the department to be communicated with, as was requested in that resolution, because I think the minister has in his department all the information that is required. All that is necessary now is to have the dredging done. I want to know from the minister whether he intends to have that dredging done this year or if he has an item in the Estimates to cover this work. It is very important and urgent that this work be speedily attended to.

We have the general vote for dredging and we have had a considerable number of representations in respect to this particular work. The matter is under consideration. Our full programme for dredging has not yet been completed and the matter will be kept in mind when the balance of the work is under consideration.

So that the minister
has not yet definitely decided whether he shall do this dredging or not? I observe that a local paper published at Antigonish states:
We have also the assurance that the Government at Ottawa will begin in a short time the opening of Antigonish harbour.
Has the minister or any of his officials given any assurance to anybody that this work was going to be attended to?
Not that I am aware of.

This is an old question. On January 26, 1912, 'Hansard' page 2202, the then Minister of Public Works, the late

Mr. Monk, referred to this very matter in the following words:
As regards the harbour at Antigonish, X shall give my hon. friend's observations every possible consideration. The demands for public works are of course very great, and it is difficult to satisfy them all, however reasonable they be. The estimates for dredging are very considerable, and the Government would not be justified in granting all the demands until we have occasion to go into the organization of our dredging and see what improvements can be made, but I shall give careful consideration to my hon. friend's request.
As far back as 1912 the late Minister of Public Works had the matter under consideration and he encouraged in the minds of the people .the belief that something would in the near future be done. Some time ago in this House, when an item was under consideration for the erection of a public building in the western part of the province, complaint was made that the minister was in the habit of putting items in the Estimates without any intention of expending the money, and in this particular instance the item had been voted and revoted for a public building although the ground had not been purchased. The minister stated that it was the intention on all occasions when he asked a vote to expend the money. I observed by the Estimates that were brought down last year, and the Estimates brought down this year -1914-1915, that there was $66,900 for Antigonish county, but I observed that $63,500 of that amount was a revote carried over from year to year. What is the idea of putting these items in the Estimates and carrying them over from year to year? Just think of it-$66,900 in the Estimates of which $63,500 is a revote! The Minister of Finance, in his Budget speech delivered April 6, 1914, said:
In considering the matter of Estimates as compared with revenue it must be kept in mind that appropriations do not always mean expenditure, partial or complete, and that on the experience of the past it may be confidently predicted that a considerable portion will be unexpended and lapse.
Is there an arrangement between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works that these items will be put in the Estimates, carried over from year to year and allowed to lapse? If so that is hardly dealing frankly with the public. It is a good deal like the way in which the farmers of Ontario, who have been the victims of the Farmers Bank, have been dealt with. Their hopes were strengthened

and they were allowed to believe that they would be paid but it turns out now that they will not be paid. It is bad enough to disappoint the people in their reasonable and legitimate demands but it is almost worse to hold out encouragement and hope that improvements are going to be made when it is not seriously contemplated to make these expenditures. I observed still further, in a letter that the Minister of Public Works wrote through his secretary on the eve of an election in Antigonish county, that there was a promise of an expenditure of $207,300 for dredging in that county. That was on December 28, 1912. The minister on that occasion wrote a letter in which he stated that he was increasing the list of items to be placed in the Supplementary Estimates to provide for expenditures in the county of Antigonish. Of course, the Supplementary Estimates had not been prepared then and they were not prepared for a long time after that but the people were encouraged to hope that these expenditures would be made last year. It turned out that not one-half, not one-tenth, scarcely a dollar, has been expended for dredging. The wharfs and breakwaters have been allowed to go to ruin, the harbours have been filling in, and my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) had to apologize the other day for the character of the steamboat service because of the inferior character of the harbours down there. They have been entirely neglected since 1911. I would ask the minister whether he has in his Estimates this year a sum for a wharf at Georgeville, and whether he is going to expend the $90,000 that he promised in his letter of September 28, 1912. Why has that not been expended? Why is not the Auld's Cove item in the Estimates of this year? So it is ail through the items for Antigonish county.
The minister, in justice to himseli, and as a matter of fair play to the people who are looking for these improvements, should state what he purposes doing. It is not enough to make promises; we want to see the cash, we want to see the money expended, and these very necessary improvements provided. I ask the minister why it is that the appropriations for a new wharf at Georgeville, $90,000, and to open the channel at Auld's cove, $15,000, have been dropped from the Estimates?
I am not aware what the reasons are; it would be impossible lor me to carry all these things in my head.
I suppose they served their purpose?
According to figures given to my hon. friend we are carrying out a great deal of work in the county of Anti-gonish, and I do not think he has much to complain about.

The minister misunderstood me. Of the $66,900 in the Estimates for 1914-15, practically all of which was voted in the Estimates of 1911-12 by the late Government, and continued from year to year without any money being expended, $63,500 is a revote, so that $3,400 has been expended in the county of Anti-gonish during the past year, in connection with the numerous wharfs and breakwaters, and other public works. I do not think the minister is giving us a fair deal, to say the least; I think we deserve better treatment from him, particularly as he was so generous on the eve of that by-election as to offer $207,000, and to go so far as to say the money would be appropriated long before the Estimates were submitted to Council. In view of the fact that he offered $207,000 to the people down there if they were good, he ought to make good his promises to some extent now.
The people were good?
They were not good in the direction the minister would like.

My hon. friend from Antig-onish has been more fortunate than I, inasmuch as the minister continues in the Estimates the appropriations for his county from year to year, but in the Estimates of 1911-12 appeared grants for the following public works in the county of Richmond, which have been dropped altogether: breakwater at Port Richmond, wharf at River Inhabitants, wharf at Louisdale, wharf at Fourchu, wharf at Soldier's Cove.
There was also a report with respect to the construction of a breakwater at Point Michaud. I understand that the site for the wharf at Fourchu was purchased since the present Government came into power. With respect to the wharf at Louisdale, tenders were called for but when the change of Government took place the contract was not awarded. I do not expect the Minister of Public Works to charge his mind with all these particular items, but I would like to know if he can to-morrow on going into
Supply give me the reasons why these items have dropped from the Estimates and no provision made for them during the present session.

A couple of years ago the department constructed a wharf at Sand Point on the Strait of Canso. The money for the construction of this wharf was voted and a suitable site for the wharf was selected by the late Government. A contract was entered into prior to the change of Government. That site was changed after the present Government came into power, and the wharf was erected at a point where the water is so shallow that the passenger steamers cannot call. The chief purpose of erecting this wharf was that the people might have the benefit of the steamer calling on its route between the town of Guysborough and the railway station	at Mulgrave.
As the steamer passes right close to Sand Point, it was thought that the erection of a public wharf at that place would be a great convenience to the people of that locality, as it would save them a drive of eight or nine miles to the railway station. There is a'daily boat passing their doors. The site of the wharf was changed to suit the politics of the district and to give $150 or $200 to a friend of the Conservative party. But the unfortunate thing is that the water is not sufficiently deep at that place, which is owned by a Conservative proprietor, for the steamer to call. It is now necessary that the minister should spend an additional sum and extend the wharf further out, so that it may be some use to the people. If the wharf had been erected at the place where the officers of the department had selected before the change of Government, there would have been sufficient water for the steamer to call; but as it is now it is useless. As some thousands of dollars have been spent upon the wharf, I wish the minister to look into the matter, and if he finds the facts stated by me to be correct, I would suggest that he provide a further additional amount to extend the wharf out into the Strait of Canso, so that it may be used.

The chief engineer has taken note of the remarks of my hon. friend. We will be glad to have the matter looked into, but I cannot believe that such a condition as that described by my hon. friend could be brought about during the past two or three years.
Progress reported.

speechtext: With the consent of the House, and before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to present the second and final report of the special committee to whom was referred Bill No. 62, an Act to readjust the representation in the House of Commons, with instructions to consider and report, and to prepare schedules containing and describing the several electoral divisions entitled to return members to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With the consent of the House I would like to read the following telegram in regard to the Empress of Ireland disaster:
H. M. S. Philomel, Survaradlo, via Ottawa,
June 5, 1914.
His Royal Highness Viceroy of Canada,
Quebec.
Being absent in the Cook islands have only Just heard of terrible disaster to Empress of Ireland, and desire on behalf of myself, my Government and people of New Zealand to convey our deepest sympathy at this terrible catastrophe.
(Sgd) Liverpool,
Governor.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Prince Edward Island-For improvements in telegraph and telephone service, $45,000.
What became of the road the hon. minister was going to build for the Montreal chaps?
What road does my hon. friend mean?
The road asked for at the annual meeting of the Motor Association. They asked the minister to put a road along there, and he said he would send an engineer.

That contract is let and
is going on.
With regard to roads and bridges, I suppose it is the intention of the department to call for tenders soon for the substructure of the interprovincial bridge across the Ottawa river at Hawkes-bury?
Instructions have already been given to call for tenders.
Can the minister say whether the right of way has been acquired from the Hawkesbury Lumber Company?
It is being expropriated.
Have the proceedings been commenced?
The chief engineer informs me that the proceedings are going on.
But the matter has not yet been decided by the Exchequer Court?
Not yet.
Can the minister tell us off-hand how many miles of telegraph and telephone lines there are under the Public Works Department?

About 6,000 miles of both in all the provinces.
Public Works-Miscellaneous, ,$1,181,150.
Who is the chief architect now?

Mr. Ewart is the chief architect yet. But I may as well say, in view of the fact that my hon. friend has asked the question, that as Mr. Ewart has grown pretty old in the service and has been a good and faithful servant of the country, it is being arranged to appoint a new chief architect, largely on the recommendation of Mr. Ewart himself, and Mr. Ewart is to be retained at his present salary as general supervisor.
Who will be the new man?
We have not any idea. If you can recommend a first-class man, we shall be glad to know of him. We want above all things a first-class architect.
I am not strong on architects.

Eegarding the item for the demarcation of the boundary line between the United States and Canada, can the minister tell us what progress has been made in arriving at a neutral zone on the international boundary line?
They are at work, and it is hoped that the work will be finished this summer. There is nothing further that I could say to my hon. friend that would be of much value.
I want to ask a question for information. What does ' metering ' the St. Lawrence river mean?

It is in connection with the discharge of the St. Lawrence, with the view of ascertaining just how much water the Americans are taking. It is necessary to have that information from an international point of view.
The flow of the St. Lawrence ?

The whole flow of the St. Lawrence.
Slides and booms, graving docks, locks and dams, etc., working expenses, etc., $181,400.
This is just the operating expenses in connection with our slides and booms.
This item for Levis graving dock has nothing to do with the new dock being built down there?	.
That is for the maintenance of the dock we have.
The present graving dock?

Yes.
Harbours and rivers, $11,690,500.
I see an item here about the French Eiver waterway improvements. Will my hon. friend tell me to what extent the work there is proceeding. Is it to be considered a start on the Georgian Bay canal?
It is an improvement of the French river, and we have let a contract, as my hon. friend knows, and it is proceeding. If is possible that another contract may be let in the near future.
Where are they working now?
At the Big Chaudiere.

That is west of lake
Nipissing?
Yes, about fifteen miles.
Has anything been done yet in lake Nipissing? How much money will my hon. friend expend there this year?
We have $500,000 in the Estimates.
That is a liberal amount for what you will spend the way you are going at it.

We are making considerable progress now.
Public Works-Ottawa-Eastern Departmental Block-Further amount required, $40,000.
How is my hon. friend getting on with this new building on Sussex street? The substructure was being constructed on force account. Is that proving pretty expensive?

The foundation has proved rather expensive. We have it completed now.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: What did it cost?
Harbours and rivers-Port Arthur and Fort William-Harbour and river improvements- Further amount required, $500,000.
What is being done at Port Arthur and Fort William?
Just carrying out the work which is continued from year to year, the breakwaters and dredging. We have to have a breakwater covering the two ports.
Is any of this extended in the river?

There is some dredging on the river.
Mr. CAEBOL'L: Is there any provision for dredging in Glace Bay? I referred to this some time ago.

The dredging at Glace bay comes out of the general vote for dredging, and we are proposing to go on with the work.
Athens- public building, $5,000.
How much will the Athens public building cost?

The contract is let at $13,800.

Chesley-Public building, $5,000.

This Chesley public
building, I suppose, is the one that was promised an South Bruce during the by-election there. They were to have a new public building and customs office. The Postmaster General also put letter boxes all over the town of Chesley. These things are going to be expensive. Unless the Postmaster General is going to adopt the policy of giving letter-boxes to all small towns, I object to his putting them in a very pretty but small town in a riding where an election is taking place. If the policy is to put them in all towns, I shall have a requisition for at least 122 places of that size, and with an equal amount of business, which require letter-boxes just as much as Chesley. But, of course, we cannot have by-elections in them all, that is the trouble. There must be some basis for the distribution of these things outside of by-elections.

My hon. friend is in error in regard to the poet office. The contract was let in April, 1912.
Mr. GRAHAM-; I was not referring to the post office. I said a public building.
It is the same thing.

My hon. friend has missed the point. It was arranged to take in the Customs Department in order to redeem the promise made by the Minister of Customs to the manufacturers of that riding. I am not objecting to that, but I object to the Postmaster General for political purposes giving letter-boxes to a certain district when he refuses them to places of equal size or larger.
This was provided for in the original contract made in 1912. We expected that the Customs department would occupy part of the building when we made the contract.
The hon. gentleman knows that many of these buildings provide space for the Customs Department, which does not necessarily occupy it at once.

That excuses the Minister of Public Works, but does not excuse the Minister of Customs. He made a promise at a very convenient time, when he need not have made it till later.
St. Jacques de l'Achigan.-Public building- revote of lapsed amount, $15,000.

When I first came to Parliament, I succeeded in obtaining the

sum of $15,000 for the construction of a post office at St. Jacques de l'Achigan in the county of Montcalm. In the session of 1911-12 the new Government withdrew this sum from the estimates, and .since then I have not ceased to make efforts to have it replaced. I have at last succeeded, and in the name of the electors of my county, I wish to thank the hon. minister of Public Works for having rendered us this justice. I see in the estimates an item of $7,000 for a public building at St. Laurent. May I ask the hon. minister for an explanation of this vote?

In regard to the first item to which my hon. friend has referred, he will remember that last year we promised to reinstate this vote which he so much appreciates. This $7,000 item is asked for to supplement the $15,000 vote placed in the Main Estimates for 1914-15. It is to make provision to complete the erection of a public building at St. Laurent on a site given free by the municipality, situate on the northeast corner of DeCelles Street and Grande Allee de Florence, with frontages of 108 feet on the former street by 112 feet on the latter. The proposed building is required for post office purposes, etc.
Do I understand that this $7,000 forms part of the $25,000 we voted last year?
Yes.
Is it for extra work?

We have not let the contract yet; this is simply to proceed with the building. In a public building of this kind we have electric fixtures, fittings, etc., to pay for.
Edmonton-New drill hall-Revote, $50,000.
Has work been begun on the drill hall?

The contract has been let and the work is proceeding.
Experimental farms-New buildings and improvements, tobacco curing stations, renewals and repairs, etc., in connection with existing buildings, fences, etc.-Further amount required, $66,800.
Are these tobacco-curing stations maintained for experimental purposes ?

This is an additional amount asked for by the Department of Agriculture. We simply put up the building; my hon. friend's question is for the Minister of Agriculture to answer.

East river-Improvements-Further amount required, $113,000.
What is this for ?
This is to finish the canal we are building at East river.

This will clean it up ?
' Mr. ROGERS: Yes.
Barachois-Extension of training pier, $700.
There are many places of that name in Nova Scotia. Whereabouts is this particular one ?

It is in the county of my hon. friend. It is asked for in a letter from John McCormick, of Sydney Mines, Nova Scotia, and W. McLeod, of Eel Cove, Nova Scotia. District engineer Bemasconi estimates the cost of the work requires $700 as follows: Extension inward, 1,500 cubic feet cribwork at eight cents, $120; extension outward, 4,800 cubic feet cribwork at ten cents, $480; superintendence, contingencies, etc., $100-making a total of $700.
Whereabouts in the county is it?

It is in the county of North Cape Breton, but I cannot say just where.
Ogden's pond-Constructing sand groin and extending channel pier, $2,800.
What sort of an extension is proposed ?

This amount of $2,800 is asked for by District Engineer Millidge for the construction of a sand groin and the extension of the pier at Ogden's Pond. Mr. Millidge states that the work consists of cutting down outer end of present work to L.W.S., rebuilding and extending a distance 30 feet to 5 feet at L.W.S.; constructing a sand groin 150 feet by 5 feet, 350 feet to the northward.

South Lake, Lakevale-Protection work,
Would the minister kindly explain this item?

This is for the construction of a brush, stone and pile protection work at the south side of the entrance of the channel to maintain the present minimum depth of water of 1} feet at extreme low water.

There was an appropriation of $12,000 to finish that job but it seems to have been lost sight of in the last year or two. Last year there was a steam dredge down there; in fact, one of the dredges was there nearly the whole of the summer, but nothing was accomplished because the harbour was filling in as fast as the dredge would scoop it up and at the end of the season they were no farther ahead than when they had begun. If the department would go ahead and finish that job once and for all at an estimated cost of something like $12,000 there would be no necessity of this tinkering and pottering.
Cape Dauphin-Boat harbour, $1,500.

Would the minister
tell me what is going to be done there?

This is to provide a
shelter for the fishermen of Cape Breton and North Victoria in the Cape Dauphin boat harbour. The chief engineer is now reporting on it.

Has he reported that
$1,500 will construct the shelter?

That is what is deemed to be necessary for the immediate protection of that harbour. I doubt if that will be enough for the completion of the work, but this amount is placed in the Estimates in order that we can proceed with it during the present year.

There is no doubt at
all that this is a very desirable work, but this is only a piece of the coast line along the Bras d'Or lakes and the only thing the minister can do is to build a breakwater which will afford shelter to the boats in behind it. It will require a very substantial structure and I have no doubt that the minister will finish the work once he begins it, but to finish it will require a vote of several times this amount.

We are making a start
any-way and we will try to finish it.
I am very glad to see in the Estimates a vote for Round Island, Mira Bay breakwater. I would like to find out from the minister if tenders will be called for the breakwater this season?

Yes, the engineers are
looking into this now and as soon as we get their report tenders will be called for. This is a very pressing work and we mean to proceed with it as rapidly as we can.

I would ask the minister to go ahead with the work this summer. A new coal company is building a line of railway to this shipping point and it is very important that the protection of the little harbour should be gone ahead with.

We understand all that.
Harbours and rivers, Quebec-Valleyfield- New wharf, $5,000.

Will the minister tell us
where the new wharf at Valleyfield will be located? .

Two applications have
been received for wharfs at Valleyfield and the report of the engineer is that the location at the upper end of the channel is the one which will be best in the public interest. It is proposed to proceed with that one at the upper end of the channel. No doubt my hon. friend understands the location there.
Have the business men and the Board of Trade of Valleyfield endorsed the view of his chief engineer in that regard?
