Mr. MeKENZIE: I wish to refer briefly to investigations held under the Inquiries Act. In Nova Scotia we had headsmen in each county, sometimes one headsman for more than one county. In North Cape Breton and Victoria, in fact all the counties of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia, we had a commissioner named Duchemin who was a very active commissioner. I understand that the Orders in Council appointing those commissioners fixed their salaries at $15 dollars a day with incidentals, and they only received $15 no rnatteT how many inquiries they conducted in one day. Mr. Duchemin is a man of my own profession, a barrister of some standing, a strong temperance advocate, a man who stands high in his church, and besides all his other virtues he is the editor of the Tory organ, the Sydney Post, in the city of Sydney. Being a prominent man and always preaching righteousness and truthfulness and honesty through his paper and on the platform, it strikes one as peculiar that there should be anything but the most rigid particularity and punctuality about anything that he would do. A man of such high standing would be expected to be very particular when he would come to deal with money matters in which he was personally interested, and wheie his own personal interests were put in contra distinction to those of the country. On September 6, 1912, Mr. Duchemin held court at a place called Big Bras D'Or in the county of Victoria. He there examined Captain George Livingstone, Captain Roderick McDonald, D. J. Morrison and H. G. McKay, Roderick Bain and Roderick McLeod. These investigations were held between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m. Under the Order in Council Mr. Duchemin would be entitled to $15 for the afternoon's services, besides his travelling expenses, etc. But I find that he submitted to the department six different bills with a full charge in every one of the bills, charging for that afternoon $128.95, while $20 would be about what he was entitled to. The items of the accounts, six of which are exactly alike, are as follows:
To travel, issuing notices, subpoenas,
etc., conducting inquiries	..	..	$15.00" Allowance for living	expenses ....	2.50" Ferry fare	05" Horse hire	
1.00
" Paid for use of room for holding
inquiries	40
" Service of witnesses	 1.00

" Stenographer copying evidence and
reports	$135
" Stationery and postage	05

The account in McKay's case is as follows:
Allowance	 $15.00
Living allowance	 3.00
Witnesses, typewriting	 5.40

These accounts cover the six cases that were tried upon the same day, totalling $128.95, whereas $21.20 would have been the proper charge. The men who were investigated and finally dismissed were my political friends, and I was keeping tab on this inquiry. I knew the day on which it was to be held, but to make absolutely sure I wrote to Captain McDonald asking him about this investigation. He writes me from Bras d'Or on the 10th March, 1913, as follows:
Big Bras d'Or, Cape Breton,
March 10, 1913.
D. D. McKenzie, M.P.,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear friend,-Yours to hand of the 8th instant, and in reply would say you were quite correct as to the date of the investigation. It was held on September 6 at three o'clock p.m., the whole being done between three and six o'clock p.m. The names of the parties who were investigated are as follows:	George Livingston, sub-collector; Rod. McDonald, preventive officer; Rory Bain, D. J. Morrison, and Rod. McLeod, boatmen; and H. C. McRay, light-keeper, Bird Island.
All those were investigated on the one afternoon at the time before mentioned.
That is the evidence I have. There is not the slightest doubt in the world about the facts being as I have stated. I submit that it is a matter of inquiry for the Government to know how its officials are conducting their business. The Order in Council appointing Mr. Duchemin allowed him a salary of $15 a day for any one day that he was out in the service of the Government, exclusive of incidentals. How is it then that he sends in a bill to the Government for $128.95, and further, how is it that the Government without any investigation paid that amount? Practically all the evidence shows that these inquiries were held on the same day, and it is strange that a business Government, as this one professes to be, did not inquire as to why these six inquiries taking place on the same day should be paid for six times. As this man Duche-man is a preacher of righteousness in many ways that I have already enumerated, it strikes one more strangely that any irregu-

laxity of this kind should be connected with him, and I think the people who read his paper, and those to whom he preaches from day to day, and those whom he addresses on the hustings should know exactly the manner in which this man deals with private and public business, and particularly public business, when it is a question of settling accounts between himself and the Government. This matter, being in my county, came very strongly before me, and without any desire of making an attack on Mr. Duchemin, I felt it my duty to warn the Government against impositions of this kind. I thought I might well bring this matter to the notice of the Government when the Estimates of my hon. friend were up.

My hon. friend has
brought up rather an important matter. He speaks of Duchemin as preaching a certain doctrine, but he does not say what church he preaches in.
I can assure my hon. friend that it is a Tory church every time.

My hon. friend asks how it is possible that Mr. Duchemin could send in such a Bill as the one he has detailed. My hon. friend complains mostly of overcharges, hut when he gets down to an-item of which he has personal knowledge he admits that Duchemin only charged this country half of what the hon. member personally knows it must have cost him. If the other items are of that nature, there is not much fault to find with Mr. Duchemin. My hon. friend also finds fault with the Government for having paid the account rendered by Duchemin. The case presented to the committee by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton is a strong one, and if bills such as he has described have been paid it is not the fault of the Government but of the Auditor General. I shall be glad to draw the attention of the Auditor General to what my hon. friend has said with a view to correcting as far as possible any mistakes that have been made.
iM.r. McKENZIE:	The information I
have given to the committee is all taken from returns brought down in this House.

If Mr. Duchemin has
been guilty of overlapping his accounts, then, undoubtedly, the Auditor General is at fault in not detecting it. The information which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) supplied the House will be taken notice of by the Auditor General, the matter will be looked into, and if any over-

lapping has taken place it will no doubt be corrected.
Of course he may be innocent, but it looks to me as if he were not.

I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to what I consider an omission in regard to the expenditure of public money at the town of Melville, Sask. This matter was brought to the attention of the minister by myself in a letter dated April 7, 1913, in which I pointed out to him that the accommodation for the post office was entirely too small for the business done at Melville and asked him to look into the question of erecting a public building at that place. In reply I received a letter from the minister to the effect that the matter would be considered. Not seeing anything in the .Estimates this year, I asked a number of questions and moved for a return of the correspondence. There is a considerable amount of it, but I will only read one letter. It is as follows:
Melville, Sask., October 12, 1912. The Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir: We respectfully beg to draw your attention to the urgent need of a Government post office building in Melville. This town has now a population of about 3,000 people and serves a very large territory. The increase of the past year has been so great that the present postmaster has had to enlarge the office .space until all the available space in the present building is now taken up. Besides, the building mow in use is owned by the local organizer of the Liberal party and there is not another "building available in Melville suitable for the purpose. It seems imperative that a Government building should be erected at as early a date as possible and we would urgently request that the matter be brought forward in the Estimates at the coming session of the House.
Very respectfully yours,
(Sgd) George Balfour, James Nixon.
Mr. Nixon was the defeated Conservative candidate. This goes to show, at all events, that attention was drawn to the necessity of providing a new public building at this important centre as far (back as October 12, 1912. But nothing has appeared in the Estimates this year for the erection of a building there. While no provision has been made for Melville, moneys have been voted for much smaller places. For instance, Kindersley, Sask., appears in the Estimates as follows:	Revote, $3,000;
1913-14, $10,000; 1914-15, 20,000. This is a town having a population of something like 
1,200. Wadena appears as follows: Revote, $10,000;	1913-14, $10,000;	1914-15, $20,000.
This is a small place having a population of between 500 and 600. It is a good little town, but it is difficult to realize that there is a necessity for an expenditure under the head of ' Public Buildings '. In the smaller places it is much cheaper to rent accommodation for the post office than to erect a monument in the form of a large public building, the greater part of which cannot be used. On the other hand, in larger places, such, for instance, as Melville, which have a future before them, a different policy is advisable. You cannot get private individuals to erect suitable buildings unless they are sure of their being continuously occupied and therefore, I submit, that the Government should erect a building in Melville suitable for the purposes of the post office and any other uses to which they may require to put it.
Now, I desire to place before the committee a few particulars illustrating the growth and importance of Melville. I do not understand what reason there can be for leaving Melville out in the cold as it is an important divisional and junctional point of the Grand Trunk Pacific and has a splendid future before it. It is a growing town. The population is now about 3,300 and the present post office is entirely inadequate for the transaction of the business there. If it is necessary to erect a public building at Wadena, surely it is more necessary in the case of a town like Melville with its growing population and fine prospects. Trains pass in and out in four different directions and there are several trains a day. The people of Melville have taxed themselves pretty heavily for city improvements showing that they have faith in the future of their town. In round numbers, they have built a town hall costing $60,000; a civic rink, $15,000; hospital, $20,000; waterworks, $80,000; electric light equipment, $60,000; street improvements, $30,000; made appropriation for sewage for 1914, $50,000; three large schools, $60,000; and one under way $20,000. In this connection, I might say that although the population of Melville requires four large schools, there is not a single child born in the town of Melville that is yet of school age, which is an example of the rapid growth of this town. A Lutheran college has been erected at the cost of $20,000 and a co-operative creamery is under way; it is expected that the projected sewage system will cost a quarter of a million dollars. Being a railway town, the

Grand Trunk Pacific has a pay roll of from $20,000 to $55,000 per month. Under these circumstances, what action has the Department of Public Works taken, or what action does it propose to take, and what reply has been made to the communications on this subject which have been addressed to the department? Here is a town of some considerable size and business importance and certainly a rented building is not sufficient to carry on the business of the post office properly. I would have thought this case would have demanded and received the attention of the department and that as a result provision would have been made for a suitable public building at Melville. If the Government had no money available it would be different, but there appears to be plenty of money for this purpose when we see a public building being erected at a cost of about $20,000 at a place like Wadena with a population of 500 or 600. I consider it my duty to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and I hope that he will rectify this omission as soon as possible.

In answer to my hon.
friend from Saltcoats (Mr. MacNutt). I would say that I quite agree with almost all he has stated in respect to the value and importance of the town of Melville. It is true, as he states, that we have omissions in connection with the erection of public buildings at various points. There undoubtedly are many omissions and they are being corrected	as	rapidly	as	itis possible for	us	to correct	them.I think I can claim that, so far as Western Canada	is	concerned,	in	theEstimates this year we are doing the best we can for public buildings at various points. As my hon. friend well knows, it is impossible to	cover them all	in	one
year. I realize that there are few places in the province of Saskatchewan that are more entitled to have a public building than the town of Melville, which is one of the most prosperous towns in the province. My hon. friend can depend upon it that he will have in me a good friend when the time and opportunity presents itself to erect a building there. I will take the earliest opportunity I possibly can to meet the wishes of my hon. friend in that respect.

I wish to know why Mr. Parent, assistant engineer in the Department of Public Works at Montreal, has been dismissed, and if a report was made against him, verbally or in writing.
I put this question before in the House, and the answer given me was that his services were no longer required. There were engineers younger than he in the department, and, if it was a question of laying off some of them, he should have been kept on, because he was one of the oldest in the service. Mr. Parent was formerly on the Georgian Bay canal, and some years ago I recommended him for the service of the department in Montreal, and, therefore, I take a special interest in him. As the deputy minister and chief engineer are present, I hope the minister will be able to give me this information.

I am not very well versed in the details of this case, but I do know that I have had very pressing requests from some of Mr. Parent's friends to reinstate him, especially from Mr. T'arte, who seems to take a very special and anxious interest in him. I am not at the moment in a position to state the exact circumstances of his dismissal, but I shall have the matter inquired into. I would be sorry, indeed, to do an injustice to Mr. Parent, if an injustice has been done. I will let my hon. friend (Mr. Verville) know what conclusion has been come to.

I think I know why Mr. Parent has been dismissed better than does the minister. A report was made against Mr. Parent, I am not sure whether verbally or in writing. The fact is that I asked him for some information which he refused to give me, but it was thought that he did give me the information, and so he was dismissed. That was absolutely unfair. I state, on my responsibility as a member of the House, that there is no truth in the allegation. If there is any member in the House, as 1 believe there is, who pressed on the department to have Mr. Parent dismissed, I tell him that it was unjust and unfair to Mr. Parent. I take the full responsibility of saying that Mr. Parent would not give me the information I asked for, and, because he was supposed to have given it to me, he was punished.
Telegraph lines-Construction of lines from Athabaska Landing to Fort McMurray; to complete, $45,000.
In what condition is this telegraph line now?

This amount of $45,000 is asked for by General Superintendent Keeley to complete the construction of a

telegraph or telephone line from Athabaska Landing to Fort McMurray.
Estimated cost-Required for constructim to end of above clearance, 41 miles at $150, $6,000; required for the further construction at $150 and lighter clearance at lowei average of $94 per mile, or together 160 miles at $244 per mile, $39,000, required for 1914-15, $45,000. The total length of the line consists as follows: Athabaska Landing (west side) to Calling river, 38 miles; to Pelican rapids, 80 miles; to House river, 40 miles; to Fort McMurray, 100 miles; total, 258 miles.
The work already done on the construction of this line is as follows: On 29th August, 1913, Superintendent R. C. Macdonald reports 57 miles of line built; outlay to date, $26,000.
On 6th November, 1913, E. D. Currier, (superintendent) reports end of Clearance 20 miles south of Pelican rapids included in above outlay, 41 miles. Construction: 57 miles at $150, say $8,500; clearance, taking balance of expenditure, $17,500; expenditure to end 1913-14, $26,000.
General Superintendent Keeley in a report dated 14th January, 1914, states that the vote for 1913-14 was applied for in continuance of the original estimate on the basis of $150 per mile. Subsequent information showed this to be altogether inadequate, because of there being no roadway clearance through the heavily timbered country. The reports herewith from the engineer in charge of construction, Mr. E. D. Currier, 6th November, 1913, and the district superintendent, Mr. R. C. Macdonald, 29th August, 1913, call lor the further sum of $45,000.
Commencing at Athabaska Landing the line would run northeasterly to Lac La-Biche. a distance of about 60 miles. There would be no difficulties encountered' in building over this section. From Lac La-Biche to House river a distance of about 100 miles is in places heavily timbered, ti** balance being covered by trees of smaller size, excepting for some small muskegs, which would offer no obstruction to building. From House river to Fort McMurray, about 90 miles, the country has been burned over leaving a large quantity of fallen timber overgrown with small second growth poplar. There is also a muskeg extending about 12 miles in this stretch.
Tamarac poles could be secured at various points along the route, and it is probable there would be no long hauls. The country is not' yet surveyed, but is reported to be well fitted for agricultural purposes; the

muskegs being of such nature that they can be easily drained. The length of the line would be approximately 258 miles. The entire absence of roads or trails north of Lac LaBiche will greatly enhance the cost of transporting material and supplies. A portion of these would have to be sent to Fort McMurray by boat and then freighted south.
(1)	The Athabaska river along which the course of the line is projected is navigable for 176 miles from Athabaska Landing to a point named Old House whence there is a trail through the woods to Fort McMurray, a distance of some 30 miles. The country to be traversed is wooded for most part hence whatever poles are required for the wire suspension will be readily obtainable.
(2)	There is a trading post at Pelican river about midway between Athabaska Landing and Fort McMurray where an office would likely serve a useful purpose. The main point of prospective traffic is however Fort McMurray itself, where there are agencies of several trading companies and some operations going on in connection with an immense asphaltum deposit and some petroleum ventures. It is also the distributing point of the Hudson Bay Company for the whole northern district and is the centre to which the entire business of the north converges.
From all of the foregoing it appears a very useful purpose would be served by the telegraph line, which could be constructed at a moderate cost and be as likely as any other in outlying districts to develop a considerable traffic, the revenue from which would materially offset the cost of maintenance.

In regard to this I think the minister should be made aware of the fact that the work on this line has not been prosecuted in a way that is at all creditable to the department. There was a vote standing in the Estimates of 1911 when this Government came into office, so that they have had the summers of 1912 and 1913, or two years of work. I understand, however, that the line is not yet completed as far as Pelican Rapids. While the progress on the line has been very slight, the expenditure has been very large.

Only $26,000 has been
spent up to date.
I think that is an abnormal amount for the length of line that has been built.
A hundred miles.

In regard to this matter I am not blaming the minister or the department except for the fact that they must have a thoroughly incompetent man in charge of the work, because otherwise the work would have been prosecuted more successfully in the time that has been available. While it is perhaps a matter with which I need not concern myself particularly, I think it, is only fair that the minister should be made aware of Che fact that a large amount of money has been expended and a very small amount of result has been achieved. There is no reason in the world why a line of 258 miles long, running alongside a navigable river for the whole distance, a river on which navigation is being carried on all the time, should take more than two years to complete. As a matter of fact, at the rate that the work has been going on so far, it will 'take more than two years more to complete the 258 miles of line.

118 miles have already
been constructed at a cost of about $200 a mile. I do not think that is a very excessive cost for the construction of a line of telegraph in a far off country such as that.
I quite agree with my hon. friend in respect to the matter of pressing the work on, because it is above all things desirable to give the people in these outlying districts the advantage and convenience of a telegraph system. I can assure my hon. friend that we shall endeavour to hurry the work forward as rapidly as possible with a view to getting this line completed to Fort McMurray, because I am fully alive to the desirability and value and necessity of such a line, particularly in view of the great trading and the developjnent of the country north and west of Fort McMurray, because as my hon. friend knows, this is practically the gateway of the great empire north of that point. In my opinion, it is the duty of the Government to see that telegraphic connection is made with Fort McMurray as rapidly as possible.

The people were very
much disappointed that this line did not reach Fort McMurray last year, and they will be very seriously disappointed if it does not get to Fort McMurray this year. Is it to be a telegraph line or a telephone line, or both? .
A telegraph line.
I would like to suggest, if it is to be a telegraph line or a telephone line, that there should be an office at Pelican rapids and another at House river.
We are bound to have an office at each of those places.

House river is about eight miles above the head of Grand rapids. I suggested to the minister last year that there should be a loop carried
10	p.m. down the river beyond House river to the head of Grand rapids, so that the transfer of freight and the change of navigation that necessarily occurs at the head of Grand rapids would be in immediate touch with telegraphic communication. It would be a pity, in view of the desirability of quick telegraphic communication from the head of Grand rapids, that the telegraph office, When the line is constructed, should be eight miles away. That difficulty could be obviated by running a loop down to Grand rapids and putting an office at that point instead of House river, which is eight miles further down. It would be carrying the wires down that far and back again. Of course it would be very nice to have an office at each place; but as they are so close together, I am not asking that there should be an office at each place; and as between the two, I think an office at Grand Rapids would serve the more necessary and useful purpose.

I quite agree with my hon. friend that we certainly should have connection with Grand rapids with our line if we are passing in the vicinity at all. The deputy has taken a note of the matter, and we will look into it.

I wish to refer to a matter that is not on the Estimates at all. I want the minister to consider himself for a moment as a court of appeal. I am going to appeal to him from his own officials. His officials will not be alarmed when they hear that their decision was in favour of the department. I suppose that they always feel safe in deciding in favour of the department as against an outside
man.	This is a small matter; but I was turned down by the officials of the department, and I never feel willing to lie down until after the last gasp.
A wharf was built at Cap Rouge in the county of Inverness last year. The contract was given, after tenders being called, to constituents of mine in North Sydney,

the name of the firm being ' Musgrave and Musgrave.' They completed the wharf and handed in the final returns to the office of the department at North Sydney, which is under the supervision of Mr. Bernas-coni. When they finished their work, as I am instructed, they handed in the final returns, and the work was accepted as completed. I want to be absolutely fair as far as the facts are concerned; if I am wrong it is not my fault. Mr. Bernasconi took the work off their hands and sent the return to the head office at Ottawa as fully completed. But between the time of the handing in of this return at North Sydney and its transmission to the head office, a storm came on and some damage was done to the work. The department insisted upon the contractors refinishing the work, which cost them an additional outlay of $150. The contract was rather severe, and I understand there has been some change since and more latitude is left to the department, so that it need not be so very rigid. When this official at North Sydney received this work as completed that ought to have been the end of it, and any damage that occurred after that should be the loss of the Government. It was only a small contract, and I think that the extra amount that wais expended would be about the measure of the profit made. I am appealing from the decision of my good friend the chief engineer, whom I know well, and who is always a good honest man., but stringent in favour of the department every time. I am appealing from him to the head of the department, who is limitless in his power, and who does not hold himself responsible to anybody but the Lord,
I suppose, and I ask the minister to take this matter into consideration and if he finds that in equity and fairness this was an act of Providence, over which these contractors had no control, he will conclude that as a matter of equity, they are entitled to the amount they claim, although under the strict letter of the contract it could be withheld. They have some other grounds, which I do not understand, but I have put the facts before the minister as accurately as I can.

I am sorry that my hon. friend should feel that he has been turned down, and, of course, if his case is as good and as clear as he appears to be able to state it, he can depend upon it we w;li see that he is turned up. We will take

note of what my hon. friend has said. It is probably true that before the engineer on the ground, who took over the work at the time, had transmitted the estimate to the head office, a storm took place and did the damage. Therefore it was not approved at head office. However, if the circumstances turn out to be as my hon. frienti states-and I presume that they are-we will undertake to see that the matter is dealt with in an equitable manner and endeavour to meet the views of my hon. friend.

In the absence of the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. Champagne) I would like to ask what is the position of the Battleford-Isle LaCrosse line. There is a revote of $9,000. I would like to have an idea how far that work has been carried and how soon it is likely to be completed to Isle LaCrosse.

The total distance, as nearly as can be ascertained, is 250 miles. From Battleford to Meadow lake, one hundred and fifteen miles, a straight road, has been constructed by the provincial Government along which our line could be built. From Meadow lake to Green lake, a turther distance of thirty-five miles, a road is now being cut out and should be ready by the time our line could be built to that point. From Green lake to Isle LaCrosse there is a cart trail following in a general way the course of the Beaver river. Between Battleford and Midnight lake, fifty-six miles, there is no timber suitable for poles. These would have to be drawn south from Midnight lake. Standard tamarac poles over this fifty-six miles, would cost delivered along the road $2.50 each. From Midnight lake northward no difficulty would be experienced in securing poles, the cost of which should not exceed $1.50 each, possibly less. There being an established trail, the cost of freighting will be less than through an unbroken country. To accommodate the various settlements, stations should be established at Jackfish Lake, twenty-five miles; Staslyn, forty-five miles; Meadow Lake, one hundred and fifteen miles; Green Lake, one hundred and forty-five miles, these distances being computed from Battleford. Between Green lake and Isle LaCrosse, at least one station would be necessary. At all these points there are already large settlements. The vote of $9,000 is asked for by the district superintendent for the purpose of completing the telegraph line from Battleford to Isle La-

Crosse. Does that cover what my hon. friend requires ?
Will the $9,000 complete ?
That is the expectation.
But my hon. friend has not said how far the line is already built. He has given a description of the road.
There is about forty-five miles to complete, out of two hundred and fifty miles.
In regard to the telegraph office at Dunvegan, for which there is a revote of $3,500, will the building accommodate anything more than the telegraph office ?

This is on the same lines as the building we are erecting at Grouard. It will accommodate a telegraph office, and there will be a certain amount of room for the operator, who will live there, and for any other public business.
It is a dwelling-house as well as an office ?
Yes.

I notice an item 'Peace River-Grand Prairie Telegraph Line-extension from Lake Saskatoon to Hudson's Hope, B. C., $41,000.' I am not going to find any fault with the department for running the line from Saskatoon to Hudson's Hope; but my information in regard to that country is that they are running the line by a very roundabout way, and over a comparatively difficult country. The telegraph line runs south from Dunvegan to Saskatoon lake, I understand, some fifty or sixty miles. The Government propose that this line, [DOT]after running south between the$e two places, shall run northwesterly from Saskatoon lake to Hudson's Hope, through a country more or less wooded and not very much opened up. On the other hand, if the line left Dunvegan and followed the cart trail all the way to Hudson's Hope on the north side, there would be comparatively no difficulty in the way of clearing or having access to the line because there is a cart trail all the way. I am astonished at this route being taken but possibly there may be some good reason for it. I should think that the natural route to take would be the direct one by Dunvegan, instead of this circuitous route.

It is evident from the report that we are taking the circuitous route
because we are following the settlement and endeavouring to meet the public requirements. It is true that probably the line is not as direct as it might be^ but it is following the localities in which there is settlement. The British Columbia Government are also pressing for this [DOT]route. Of course, my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has the advantage of having personal knowledge of this country which very few of us have, and in view of what he has said we shall certainly be glad to look into it again.

I am not objecting, I just wondered why the line is being constructed in that way. I am very pleased to see the Government constructing the line to Hudson's Hope. It is at the head of navigation on the Peace river, it is in British 'Columbia and it is very desirable to have connection with that place by telegraph.

I asked my hon. friend yesterday to bring down a few facts and data as regards the rural mail delivery. I would like to know first how the service stands by provinces. I know that Ontario 'has been quite responsible in this matter and I believe that in New Brunswick and the West there has been a demand for the establishment of rural mail routes. I know that these rural mail delivery routes will be highly beneficial to the people and therefore, I would be very pleased if my hon. friend could see his way clear to stimulating our own people in Quebec. There I know that the circumstances are *somewhat different. The farmers generally congregate on Sundays at the church door and the post office is open during an hour or so after divine service and the mail is distributed there. But all this is a matter of education. The farmer of Quebec would be responsive to this system if he understood the great benefits to be derived by the distribution of literature on farming and also by having a daily paper.
Perhaps it would be well for the officers of my hon. friend's department to inform the people in our province of the advantages of that service. Some routes have been opened up in the eastern townships of Quebec and the people are very pleased with the system. I know that farmers in one or two places in my own county petitioned for the opening of rural mail routes which have since been granted. That 'shows that

some interest is being taken in the matter by our farmers. I think the minister should carry on a campaign of education as to the advantages of rural mail delivery so that the system 'would not be confined to one or two provinces as it is at present.
I come now to the question of cable rates. My hon. friend knows what interest those of us who have been journalists take in this matter. Not very long ago Sir John Willison, the correspondent of the London Times, wrote a series of articles for his newspaper which have been reproduced in all of the overseas dominions pointing out the danger of the Americanization of the press of this countrj. There is no doubt that our press is more or less inspired by the news collecting agencies of the United States. If we are in danger of Americanization it is not so much from the introduction of American sports but from the transmission of telegraphic despatches to our newspapers through American channels. Be that as it may, it is certain that if we had cheaper cable rates we could obtain a better mews service from the British Isles. In this connection, I wish to again call the attention of my hon. friend to the British magazine post which I succeeded in establishing in 1906. Previous to that time, we had received a mere few thousand pounds of British magazines and newspapers each year, but after the arrangement of 1906 between the Post Office Departments of Canada and Great Britain our consumption of British magazines and papers increased to 600,000 pounds a year, and our British settlers in the Northwest Territories, and in fact all over Canada, were enabled to keep in touch with home. The circulation of English papers and magazines in this country helps to develop a spirit of fraternity between Canada and the old land, and it would be a thousand pities if because of a little difference between the two post office departments, the British magazine post were to be done away with. I sincerely hope that my hon. friend will do his best to continue the arrangement made in 1906. The other day I was reading in the Monthly Circular, Empire Press Union, a letter, dated August 9, 1913, to the News-Advertiser, Vancouver, B.C., from M. A. C. Cummings, containing the following paragraph:
We have a cheap cable rate to Australia and the newspapers here, with one exception, have their own cable services from the Commonwealth. With Great Britain it is different.

Few of the Canadian journals can afford the cable tolls from London, consequently they depend almost entirely on British cantes as despatched by American correspondents in London to their newspapers in New York and Chicago. The results are sometimes amusing. We get intimate ' facts ' of the doings of Duchesses and ' quarrels ' In the Royal family, thinly-veiled jokes at the monarchy, and the popularity of the ' tango ' and ' turkey trot ' in London ballrooms, but we never hear a word of the doings of the Imperial Parliament-unless they interest Americans for the moment- or of the great developments, social and political, that are going on throughout England.
Another independent opinion was given in the same paper by Mr. M. E. Nichols of the new (Montreal Daily Mail. He says:
I hope the day is not far distant when the Canadian newspapers will co-operate to the extent of bringing a comprehensive cable service direct from Great Britain and spare the Canadian public the American made and American edited cable service upon which the Canadian Press is at present largely dependent.
I need not dwell any longer on this point, except to remind my hon. friend that last year he promised Parliament that he would be able to give this country much cheaper rates by reason of the establishment of the Poulsen wireless system. Perhaps my hon. friend would tell the committee what has been done with regard to that, and whether the Poulsen system will soon be in operation. Of course there may be a little exaggeration in the letters I have just read to the House. Undoubtedly such important papers as the Gazette of Montreal, the Globe, and the Mail and Empire of Toronto, the Ottawa Citizen, the Manitoba Free Press and a few others have an excellent news service, but these exceptions only prove the rule. The country press cannot get the best news because we have not a cheap cable service. When this matter was up in the House before, I expressed the opinion that the day was not far distant when Canada would have a state-owned cable on the Atlantic as well as on the Pacific. Undoubtedly the Pacific cable between Australia and Canada has done much to cheapen cable communication between the two countries. Perhaps the wireless system will attain to such a state of perfection that it will be an excellent substitute. My hon. friend the Postmaster General has a grand idea about this; he has been working for the last iwo years towards jthe establishment of the Poulsen wireless system.

That the parcel post will be of little use in affecting the cost of living will certainly be evident to any one who will study its provisions. Housewives who have visions of chickens and eggs coming in by parcel post might ae well abandon such expectation. Such things will have to be produced within twenty miles of the Montreal post office, because the parcel post rate beyond that distance is considerably in excess of the express rate. The Dominion Express Company, not longer than a month ago, issued a notice to its patrons and agents asking them to be generous to the parcel
post, and stating that it was not afraid of its competition. Therefore, we are in this position that, while in the United states the express companies go out of business because of the parcel post, in this country the express companies have asked their patrons and agents to encourage parcel poet, because they are not afraid of the competition. A criticism of the parcel post system has been made of late by an authority, Mr. A. W. Marble, president of the Merchants' Association of New York, who says that:
The limitations of the parcel post are these:
It does not provide a * pickup ' service.
It does not adequately provide for safety.
It does not provide adequate indemnity for loss.
It does not provide any indemnity for damage.
It excludes a wide range of commodities from quick transportation.
It prevents valuable packages from being securely closed.
It is obvious that unless all these limitations be removed the parcel post cannot effectively serve numerous imperative transportation needs.
However, we must, in spite of all this criticism, encourage my hon. friend in developing and expanding as much as possible the parcel post system in Canada. It is a good beginning, it can be improved upon, and my hon. friend, I know, is sufficiently alive to present conditions to understand that he must do something for his country and for the consumer. My hon. friend referred to the question of cable rates and asked me where we stood on the Poulsen contract, which is a very interesting question. The installations both at Ballybunion on the coast of Ireland and at Newcastle in New Brunswick are almost completed. They would have been completed by the first of this month, had it not been for the fact that a serious accident took place which has delayed the final installation of one of these stations. I have received word that this accident may cause a delay of one or two months. We do not propose to go into the question of

a new Atlantic cable until we have seen the result of this installation. The home Government have represented to us that they will not join with Canada, New Zealand and Australia in regard to the question of an Atlantic cable until we all know more about the very extraordinary progress which wireless telegraphy is making throughout the world. In the first place, they have represented to us that two cables will have to be laid in order to have a complete and safe service. In the second place they say: We may have gone to very great expense in laying two or three cables and then find that in the end we might have had as good if not better service by wireless. I did my best when I was over in England to get them to join in that proposition, with the result that protracted negotiations were entered into. When we know more about wireless telegraphy, we may have to go into the cable question again; but for the moment, we are not disposed to look into it any more until we know what wireless will give us.
As regards the question of the British magazines to which my hon. friend has referred, I am not going to budge one inch from the position I have taken in regard to this matter. I am sure I am right. We have been giving for seven years free transportation for British magazines; and whilst we were doing that all the way from Liverpool to Vancouver, the British Government were collecting one penny for the transportation of these magazines for a distance of 220 miles from London to Liverpool. Is it reasonable to ask Canada again to enter into such an arrangement? It does not appeal to me as a business proposition, and I am not going to assent to it. I have made a very fair proposition to the British Government, and I think it will be accepted. I have asked that one-half of that penny should come to Canada for transporting the British magazines a distance of five or six thousand miles, and that the British Government should keep the other half for transporting the magazines a distance of 220 miles. If that is not fair, I do not know what fairness is. Canada should certainly get something for the transportation of these British magazines. At that rate the British magazines will again have a good deal of preference over the American magazines, which is just what we want; but we ask the British post office to share with us the revenue which it is receiving. I have lately received a letter from the Brit-

ish Postmaster General informing me that he thinks we will be able to arrange the matter. Therefore I see with a good deal of pleasure that he is not being too much encouraged by the stand which my hon. friend took some time ago on the floor of the House, when he practically told the British Postmaster General that he should not assent to our proposition. I do not see why Canada should bear the whole burden in this respect, and get nothing for doing so. If my hon. friend the member for Rouville does not see it 11 p.m, in that light, I fail to understand from what angle he looks at the question, or what other reason he has for coming to the conclusion that the British post office, which is much richer than ours, should get the whole benefit from the carrying of the magazines and that we should get nothing. I have very often asked myself by what method of reasoning my hon. friend has come to that conclusion, and I am still at a loss to understand it.
In regard to parcel post, my hon. friend has criticised this in a mild way, and I might say, in a fair way. He has been much fairer in regard to parcel post than the newspapers throughout the country belonging to his party have been. There has been throughout this country an organized war against parcel post. I do not know why this should have happened; but I have collected articles published in all the weekly Liberal papers in Canada, and they are exactly the same, word for word.
There is the same feeling throughout the country.

And the same feeling is expressed in the same words. It is a most extraordinary thing. It is a regular war against parcel post. The hon. member for Rouville, who occupies a responsible position, has told u-s to-night that parcel post is a good thing and should be encouraged; yet these papers, one after another, tell us that it is an awful thing. I am not going to read these articles to the House; I will keep them as souvenirs. On a question like this-there is nothing in it for me-I think both parties might unite and try to make a success of it. I suppose my hon. friend will be happy to hear that this regular campaign in the press against parcel post has had its effect,

but nut to the extent which I suppose those people who wrote these articles might have wished. Our parcel post system is in fair shape; it is working well; it is developing steadily, even while receiving all these black eyes and while probably a good many Liberals in the country, after reading these articles, must have said to themselves: Let us not use the parcel post because a Tory Government has inaugurated it. Sometimes when I have asked people as to how the parcel post system is working in their districts, they have said: Well, in our district the majority are Liberals and they are not going to use parcel post, because the papers have said it should not be used. That shows that this campaign has had its effect. Is it a noble effect? Is it something that ought to be encouraged? I am not going to discuss this question to-night, because, for one thing, it is too late in the session, and, moreover, I do not think it should be discussed at all. It is obviously an anti-Canadian stand. It has not had the success it might have had, and I hope
it will not continue; but even if it does, we are assured of a successful parcel post in spite of all this opposition.
We are assured of the success of parcel post in spite of all this. We have not been able to judge in the department. We put the parcel post policy into effect on the 10th of February. We have not had sufficient time to say what the result is, but from what reports we have there is a steady increase and the people are availing themselves of it more and more every day.

I am also going to put on ' Hansard ' a very complete statement prepared under the supervision and to a great extent the work of the deputy Postmaster General, which puts the whole of this question in a fair way and gives to the public all the information which it is necessary to have in this respect. It is something that the members of the House should have on ' Hansard ' in order to know all the details:
The Postmaster General is informed, in reference to the rates charged by the express companies as compared with the rates brought into existence by the inauguration of parcel post, that whilst in the greater number of cases the parcel post rates are lower, it must be confessed there are some points where, owing to special circumstances, the express companies' charges are a few cents lower on the larger parcels. On all parcels up to seven pounds, however, the parcel post rates are very decidedly a decrease on those charged by the express companies. The rate is very decidedly in favour of parcel post on all parcels up to three pounds, and is lower than the express rate up to seven pounds, although the difference in the last three pounds is not so marked as in the first three pounds. It must be borne in mind, however, that no matter how minute the parcel or how short the distance it is sent by an express company, the minimum charge is twenty-five cents. This gives the express companies an enormous price on all very small parcels. This is not the case in parcel post, as we allow parcels to be posted at one cent an ounce up to ten ounces. If the department were to even make a minimum charge of ten cents it would be an immense financial gain as regards carrying out the scheme of parcel pqst hut it has been decided to give the public the advantage of the old rate of one cent an ounce on all parcels ten ounces or less-up to ten cents, which is the minimum of our charges per pound, outside the local rate.
Moreover, the maximum charge that can be made on any parcel up to eleven pounds, no matter what the distance, is twelve cents per pound. This is a very much lower rate than that of the express companies. This can perhaps be better illustrated by an example:
Take an eleven-pound parcel. The express charge thereon from Montreal to

Calgary is $1.60; under the parcel post rates the charge will be $1.32; and if the parcel is taken further, from Montreal to Vancouver, the discrepancy in the charges becomes greater. The express parcel would be paid for at the Tate of $2, for eleven-pound parcel, or a fraction over eighteen cents a pound, whereas under parcel post the amount paid would be $1.32, a maximum of twelve cents per pound. Another instance-on an eleven-pound parcel from Montreal to Winnipeg the parcel post rate will be ninety-two cents, the express rate $1.25. The only places where the express rates would seem to be more favourable than our rates is in the case of the larger parcels from seven to eleven pounds sent to points where there is competition between two or three express companies, notably, between Montreal and Quebec, or Montreal and Toronto. The express on an eleven-pound parcel from Montreal to Quebec is forty cents, and the parcel post rate will be forty-eight cents. Between Montreal and Toronto the express rate on an eleven-pound parcel is forty-five cents, and the parcel post charge will be sixty-eight cents, but on all parcels under seven pounds, even between these points, the parcel post rates are the lower, and, when you take into consideration the fact that the minimum parcel post rate for one pound is only 10 cents, as compared with 25 cents by express, and that on all parcels up to ten ounces only one cent an ounce is charged, instead of a minimum charge of 25 cents, the advantage in favour of parcel post, if worked out, would be very great indeed. Moreover, from the fact, as stated above, that all parcels under seven pounds have the advantage under the parcel post rates, and the experience of the United States since the inauguration of parcel post, that the average parcel sent through the mails is three pounds or under, it will be seen that, in the practical working out, an immense boon has been conferred on the people, and that a much reduced rate on parcels sent through the mails has been given to the people of Canada.
The charges on all parcels up to and including seven pound parcels between Montreal and Quebec are lower under parcel post than by express.
Between Montreal and Toronto, the charges on all parcels up to five pounds are in favour of parcel post; on six pounds

the same rate; and from seven to eleven pounds the express rate is lower.
Between Montreal and St. John, parcel post has the lower rate up to nine pounds; after that the express rate is a little lower.
Taking Toronto, in the province of Ontario, as a centre-all charges, of course, from Toronto to Montreal and Quebec will be just the converse of what has been quoted from Montreal as a centre, giving practically the same results; hut from Toronto to Winnipeg the parcel post rate is very much lower than the express on all weights. From Toronto to Regina, Toronto to Calgary, to Vancouver and Edmonton, the parcel post charges are very much lower on all weights.
It is only, therefore, at certain points where, owing to geographical conditions and competition, the express companies have been compelled to produce a very low rate, that there is any advantage in favour of the express companies as regards charges made to the public. After having crossed the border from one zone to another, as all charges under the parcel post system are flat rate charges, the charge must be made to every part of the province the same. This is not necessarily the case with the express companies, which, not being a Government organization, but private companies, have much greater elasticity in their formation, and are able to temper their charges to meet local conditions. As, between Toronto and Hamilton-whereas we must make the same charge from Toronto to Hamilton as to all other points of the province, the express companies, being private concerns, are enabled to make charges much lower than the Post Office Department could do, as we have not the same elasticity, but even here the rates are in favour of parcel post on parcels up to and including four pounds. On five pound parcels, the parcel post charges are one cent higher than the express rates; on six pounds, the same; and on parcels over seven pounds to eleven pounds the parcel post rates are higher. I quote this case because it is an extreme case, as being the most favourable-owing to the size of the two cities and their contiguity-to the express companies and the least favourable to the Post Office Depart ment.
From Toronto to Ottawa, the parcel post rate is lower in all charges on weights up to nine pounds; a little higher on the ten . and eleven pound weights.
From Toronto to Quebec, the parcel post 331J
charges are lower up to nine pounds, and a little higher on the ten and eleven pound parcels.
From Toronto to St. John, the parcel past charges are lower up to eight pounds, and a little higher than the express charges from eight to eleven pounds.
From Toronto and Montreal to Halifax, the charges under the parcel post system are lower than the express companies' charges on all weights up to eleven pounds.
To recapitulate, on all weights up to eleven ounces the parcel post charge is one cent an ounce, the express charge is 25c on each parcel, even on one ounce, no matter what it weighs. Up to one pound, the parcel post charge is 10c; the express rate, 25c. On all parcels up to five or six pounds, outside of the exceptions above enumerated, the parcel post charges are considerably lower than the express rates. On weights over seven pounds and up to eleven pounds, in some few instances the express charges are lower than those under parcel post, but in the majority of instances, even in these weights, the parcel post is much the lower rate, so that taking it on the whole, it means that the people of this country are going to have their parcels carried at a rate representing thousands of dollars less than has been taken from them in the past by the express rates which have been charged in Canada.
Moreover, an additional advantage in parcel post over the express companies is in the fact that a parcel delivered in one post office in Canada is taken to any other post office in Canada under a fixed single rate, whereas if it goes by express and if the express company going to destination differs from the express company at the office of origin, then at least two, or perhaps three charges may be made. This, of course, is absolutely avoided in the parcel post system.
The area of distribution by the express companies is confined to cities and towns, whereas the area of distribution of parcel post not only embraces cities and towns but extends to all our rural delivery routes and all post offices throughout the Dominion. The area of distribution, therefore, is infinitely larger; there is only one charge from one part of the Dominion to another; and the rates charged are on the whole infinitely less than the rates charged by the express companies. The area of distribution is much vaster, the number of post offices to which distribution is made being fourteen thousand, as against five

thousand odd by the express companies; delivery is effected on two thousand one hundred and three rural free delivery routes-representing some ninety thousand people to whom distribution is made-and on all other mail routes throughout the country.
As regards routes such as between Hamilton and Toronto, where the advantage is with the express companies, there will be no intereference with these, and the people of course will have the benefit of both systems. The object of parcel post is not competition with the express companies, nor with any other class of carriers, but simply to give the people a safe, reliable and cheap transportation of the necessities of life.
R.M. Coulter,
Deputy Postmaster General.
I think I have touched on all the points mentioned by my hon. friend.

Can my hon. friend
state what the approximate cost entailed by the establishment of the parcel post is, and what is the number of extra employees?
We have not had to get many more employees. We have been obliged to get several clerks in important city post offices, and a few additional railway mail clerks.

Any carriers in the
cities?

We have in important cities-in fact, in all the cities where we have letter carrier delivery-parcel post delivery. I have in mind that, sooner or later, after I have had. further consultation with my officers and the superintendents of the parcel post, we shall not only deliver the parcels as we are doing now, but shall collect them as well. I do not know what my officers will say about it; they have devoted a good deal of time and attention' to the organization of this scheme, and I shall be largely guided by their advice. But I have it strongly in my mind that our system will not be complete until we collect parcels as well as deliver them, that is, in the cities served by letter carriers.

We have here a general store, a blacksmith shop, a sawmill, a feed mill, a planing mill and our chapel. So people come here to get their mail, as well as to transact other business.
He had been in charge of the post office for nine years; he had not even the right to vote, for that territory is still unorganized, and it is not a large village, since there is no resident priest. The letter goes on:

Despite our protests, we were deprived of our post office all the same, which was located at the far end of a range, four miles from the village, in a place where there are only a few families to make use of it. Between the spot where the office is located at present and Ste. Agathe, there are only four families settled; the mail carrier passes in front of those four houses only, while formerly, when the post office was located in the village, the mail carrier passed in front of the houses of almost every family in the place. People had to come for their letters, but when they had letters to post, they only had to hand them to the mail carrier on his way. To-day, on the contrary, we have to drive a distance of five or six miles to post a letter.
And he closes his letter as follows:
Hoping that you will And your way to secure for us another post office or to have the old post office restored, or else have the present postmaster to move to the village, I remain. ' Tour, etc.,
Mdnasippe PichA
And that is what is termed justice. I call it tyranny to remove the post office from a village and locate it in a back section where there are only four families settled, just for the purpose of putting out a poor man. It is no wonder if tyranny is complained of, after all the postmasters and all the mail carriers have been dismissed on account of their Liberal leanings.
I cannot obtain from the authorities the establishment of routes for rural mail delivery, and I am satisfied that it is the result of political bias and nothing else.
When the hon. Postmaster General states that our intercourse has always been friendly, he is right, but he is under the influence of the man I defeated and whom I shall defeat once more if he opposes me. He cannot get over his defeat. Henceforth, I shall have two constituencies: the one I represent and the one where my folks have been living, where I was born, and I am quite certain that my majority will be increased fourfold.

If the hon. gentleman had read this correspondence, how could he make such a statement to the House? Mr. Denison had been postmaster of Richmond for a number of years. The Liberal party did not cut off anybody's head to make room for him. In 1895, the Conservative Government voted a sum of money for a public building in the town of Richmond, and the building was not completed until after the Liberal party came into power. A postmaster was required. Mr. Denison was recommended for the position, and got it. There was no politics in that case; no one lost his head through Mr. Denison being appointed. Hon. L. P. Pelletier,

Honourable Sir,-In the matter of the dismissal of Postmaster Denison, of Richmond, P.Q. I was astonished to read that you had been accused of [DOT] brutality ' by the member from Richmond and Wolfe, Mr. E. W. Tobin. I deem it my duty to draw your attention to certain facts which may go to show matters in an entirely different light. The imputation of brutality comes with poor grace from a Liberal member of Parliament when the treatment meted out to Mr. C. C. Campbell former postmaster at Richmond and Mr. Denison's predecessor in office is recalled.
As you are aware the Richmond office was one of the first established in the Eastern Townships In 1817 and has had for postmasters successively:
Stephen Bernard, 1817; Arthur Lord, 1819; John P. Dresser, G. K. Poster, 1837 ; Herb. Foster, 1880; C. Campbell, 1888 ; and the expostmaster Mr. Denison, 1898 to 1914.
Now, some time prior to 1896, the growing requirements of Richmond necessitated the building of a new office to replace the old one and a branch office at the railway station of which Mr. Jutras (deceased) was postmaster. When the Liberals came to power in 1896 the new office was ready for occupancy and Mr. C.
C.	Campbell the senior postmaster was the legitimate heir to the appointment, or rather was legitimately entitled to be transferred to the new building.
Mr. Campbell had been a clerk in the ' G. K. Foster post office ' for years, both under Mr. G. K. Foster and his son Herbert Foster; he had been deputy postmaster under the latter and finally was postmaster from 1888 to the time of his dismissal. Young, active and fully qualified he had given good public service; he was a poor man with a growing family and needed the emoluments.
No charges or no investigation of political par-

tisanship or incompetency were lodged against him. On the contrary, he was very generally supported throughout the town and tributary district of which Richmond is the distributing point. Many of his strongest supporters at the time were Liberals; there are men who hold high office in the Quebec Government to-day and men in the public service; others who have passed away; others still who are prominent in public life in Richmond and high in the councils of the Liberal party, who did everything in their power to prevail on the then Postmaster General, Mr. Mulock, to retain Mr. Campbell in office. One group of ten leading Liberals journeyed to Montreal to advise the leaders there against an unjust dismissal; a petition signed by over 325 electors, and including a great list of prominent Liberal leaders and followers, was sent to the hon. Postmaster General Mulock in Mr. Campbell's interest. This memorial sets up: 1st. That it was the desire of all that no change be made in the postmastership; 2nd. That Mr. Campbell had not been guilty of partisanship in the late election (1896) ; 3rd. That he was a satisfactory, competent and experienced officer who by reason of his long connection (27 years) and good service in the old Richmond office, was entitled to the new one. All to no avail. Mr. Denison, who had been postmaster at a small office at Denison's Mills since 1861, who had been a defeated candidate in 1896 against the late Mr. Joseph Bedard, who was not the unanimous choice of his party and in spite of the representations already stated, Mr. Denison who was a well-off farmer, who had no special qualifications for the office, must be provided for. His son, Mr. W. O. Denison, was given the postmastership of Denison's Mills which his father held almost uninterruptedly since 1861, and Mr. Denison, sr., was given the Richmond office in 1898.
Does it appear to you that there was much 4 mercy ' shown Mr. Campbell by the party which is now crying 4 cruelty ' through Mr. Tobin.
You will kindly note that Mr. Campbell did not ask to be reinstated himself as he might have legitimately done; neither does his letter of February 11, 1914, ask for Mr. Denison's dismissal; it is simply a statement of facts susceptible of proof, and which your department deemed sufficiently important to investigate. The result of the investigation would go to show that there was ground for complaint. The evidence given by Mr. H. Leonard and by Mr. C. Miller will scarcely be questioned by Mr. Tobin ; both Liberals, one a prominent business man of the town, Mr. Leonard, an ex-Liberal candidate, and a man not given to complaining without reason. It would appear from the above facts that a large number of very prominent Liberals were opposed to Mr. Denison's nomination from the outset; it further appears that at the time of his dismissal his Liberal friends had concluded that he was unable to discharge the duties of such an important office as Richmond to the public satisfaction.
Because Mr. Campbell had been unjustly dealt with would be no excuse for the dismissal of his successor; Mr. Campbell has not shown any revengeful spirit; the conditions of which he and others complained of were gradually getting worse, yet nothing was said until the whole public of Richmond were complaining of the state of affairs at the office; through
physical incapacity, or through sheer inability by reason of advancing age, Mr. Denison had become unable or unwilling to preserve order in the lobby. It would have been a simple matter for him to lodge evidence with the proper authorities against any act of vagrancy, mutilation of property, or disorderly conduct. When he applied to the Town Council for police protection his appeal was unaccompanied by any evidence or charge which an officer could act upon ; although he put in many hours daily in the office he appears never to have seen anything of what was going on-again evidence of inability or reluctance to act.
The real truth of the disorder in the lobby was that a number of boys behaved badly there; Mr. Denison's loss of control alone prevented him from administering the proper remedy. Over a year ago, a prominent Liberal here asked me why a change was not made in the office on account of the incompet-er.cy of Mr. Denison-and the poor service. If I have made my meaning clear you will have seized the contrast in the manner in which Mr. Campbell and Mr. Denison have been treated:
1.	Mr. Campbell, young, competent, poor and needful of the office, supported by both parties, no charges against him ; no investigation, dismissed by the 4 gentle ' Liberals.
2.	Mr. Denison, rich, who did not need the office, opposed by Liberals at the start and declared incompetent by both parties at the end, Mr. Denison who had already had an office which his son still occupies; requested to resign, refused, dismissed after departmental Inquiry. Surely the Denisons, father and son, have been well treated by both parties since 1861.
If there be any 'cruelty' in connection with this dismissal it would be the case for Mr. Denison to say: 4 O Lord deliver me from my friends.' I wish to add that as a citizen and a man Mr. Denison stands well in the esteem of his fellow citizens.
I notice, in the debate, that Mr. Bureau made reference to me as 4 the man that Tobin liked '. In justice to Mr. Tobin I want to say that Mr. Tobin never did anything of the kind. I presume what Mr. Bureau meant was that in the election of 1911 Mr. Tobin got more votes than I did. What happened in my case, happened to the vast majority of the Liberal candidates in that election. It seems to be the fate of political struggle, so much so that in the county of Richmond and Wolfe, no less a distinguished statesman than the present leader of the Opposition Sir Wilfrid Laurier was. .	. .
what shall I say? Defeated by C. C. Clevelai*! some years ago.

I understand that the Postmaster General is increasing the compensation to the railways on account of their having to carry parcels. I have had several inquiries from mail couriers in my county as to whether it is the intention of the Postmaster General to give them extra remuneration for the extra services they

perform in connection with the parcel Dost.

The question is a fair one. The couriers who had contracts previous to the coming into operation of parcel post and whose contracts consequently did not cover parcel post, are entitled to a proportionate increase, if the weight of mail which they carry is increased. We have had already several requests in that respect, which we are considering.

What system has the Postmaster General adopted to enable him to arrive at a conclusion as to the proportionate increase that should be paid? Is he asking the couriers to supply returns as to the number of parcels they are carrying?

We ask the officers and the postmasters at the points where the couriers start and at the points of destination. In cases where the demand seems a little large, we send one of our officers to verify the facts.

Is it necessary for the couriers to make application for this increased renumeration in respect of parcel post, or are they advised by the post office inspector that they are entitled to that increased remuneration?
We have taken it for granted so far that those who are entitled to the increase will ask for it.
Some of them might be afraid, perhaps that their contracts would be cancelled if they asked for the increase.
No, their contracts will never be cancelled when they make application like that.
What is the exact meaning of these words 'new rates? Is it the increased subsidy to the railway?

Yes, and it changes its basis. Formerly it was a contract per track mile; and these new rates are per car mile.

I am glad to see that the Minister of Public Works has implemented the promise he made to me some months ago that in the new buildings he would set apart a suite of rooms for the annual meeting of the Royal Society of Canada. This society was founded by the Marquis of Lome when he was Governor General, and part of its expenses is borne by the Government; it is a state society, so to speak. Its annual meetings are held in Ottawa, sometimes in the Carnegie Library and sometimes in the Normal school both places, unfortunately, not suited to its requirements. An annual volume is issued, containing the various papers contributed by the society, which is published by the Government. A motion was passed last year at the annual meeeting-I happen to be a member of the society myself-to the effect that the Government shouild provide room for the society, and I have had practically the promise of my hon. friend that something would be done. Possibly in the new buildings he intends to set apart a
suite of rooms. If he does so it will be perfectly satisfactory to me and to the fellows of the Royal Society as well.

At the present time a room is supplied in the Museum for the Royal Society, and it is not as desirable as we should like it to be. But my hon. friend can depend upon it that when we are making our plans I will see that suitable rooms are provided for the Royal Society.

The reason I ask for a suite of room is that the society is made up of various groups. There is the English section, the French section, the scientific section, the natural history section, and so on, all of which meet in different rooms. At times all of the groups come together in a general meeting. I should be pleased if my hon. friend would arrange a suite of rooms, one for their library, one for their secretary, and others for the meetings of the various sections.

I happen to read the French * Hansard ' because I take some interest in it, as I should, being a member of the French-Canadian representation in this House. We all take a certain pride in our mother tongue, and I am bound to say that although most of the translators are excellent, still there are a few who are not up to the mark. Yesterday I was reading the translation of a speech which I delivered

a week ago on the Farmers Bank and the Bank Ville Marie, and I discovered any number of faults and mistakes in the translation. I do not wish to censure the Speaker, far from it; but it seems to me that the Debates Committee has lost all power, and its existence is valueless to the House and to ' Hansard.' In former times the translators were called before the committee, underwent examination, and were selected by the committee. This has been done away with, and I must say that the change has not improved our French ' Hansard.' It is bad enough. I have no right, as a member of the loyal Opposition, to make any suggestions to my friend the Speaker; but his friends will tell him that I have possibly some knowledge of the French language; I claim to have some little knowledge of it; and the Speaker may believe me when I tell him that our French ' Hansard ' is not what it should be, because it lacks a director. On different occasions I have suggested the appointment as chief of that staff of an old friend of members on both sides of the House, Mr. Lucien Lasalle. He is not a political friend of mine; he is a good Conservative; hut he has not taken any part in politics for years. He is now senior of the staff and is admittedly one of the ablest translators I know of. How is it that he is passed over and ignored and a new man, also a personal friend	of	mine, Mr.	Trudel, is
appointed as acting chief translator?
Why	was	not	the senior,	and alsoone of	the	ablest translators	appointed?Friends	of	His	Honour the Speaker
will tell him that Mr. Lasalle has all the qualifications. It may he true that of late he has only had the use of one aTm, but that does not prevent him from discharging his duties efficiently. I am making these suggestions in the interests of those who read the French Debates, and I would humbly suggest that Your Honour be good enough to reconsider your decision in this matter. I am not passing judgment on Mr. Trudel. He is a very old friend of mine -we have known each other ever since we were at the university together-but Mr. Trudel will himself admit that he is not in line with Mr. Lasalle as a translator. I am sure that the Conservative members of this House would approve of Mr. Lasalle being appointed. He has been engaged in active journalism for over forty years, and has been a translator here for the last thirty years. He has the necessary ability, and if he were appointed chief I am sure

he would be a credit to the staff, and ' Hansard ' would read much better. He is the oldest translator, and knows the ropes thoroughly. In 1896, I appeared before the Debates Committee on behalf of Mr. Lasalle. Some hon. gentlemen wanted to have him dismissed because he had been taking part in politics, but I suggested to the committee that we should forget the past and consider Mr. Lasalle on his merits. The committee, then presided over by the late Senator Ellis, said: Very well, he shall remain on the staff, hut he must not take part in politics in the future. Mr. Lasalle has faithfully discharged his duties since that time. There are many translators as able as he, but he is the senior, and for these reasons I suggest that he be appointed.
