He said: Mr. Speaker, as the hour is late, I do not wish to detain the House, and will offer only a few remarks. There is no doubt that the present Minister of Militia has inaugurated an era of extravagance. The expenditure for militia has increased by several millions since he became the head of the department. For a peaceful country like Canada, I think it is absurd to spend $14,000,000 on militia. We are not threatened with invasion, there is no neighbouring country that threatens to invade Canada; and I submit that to spend $14,000,000 on militia is a



foolish expenditure, when the country needs so much money for development, and when public works are demanded in every part of the country. The Government says that the revenues are not sufficient to build all the railways and public works needed, but they have enough money to 6pend on useless drill halls in small places, where there -are only four. or five hundred of a population, as was demonstrated by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the other day. The Minister of Militia finds money to take junketing tours through Europe with an anny of colonels and lieutenant colonels and honorary colonels, spending $25,000 of the good money of this country. iHe finds money to pay useless officers at headquarters, staff, officers who do not earn onehfth of their salary. Their main work is to go around in gold lace uniforms and to frequent the clubs. In fact, it became so notorious that last year even a Conservative newspaper, the Citizen, called them the 'Scotch and soda officers.' It seems that their main occupation is to go to the clubs. The Rideau Club is full of them; they go there to talk military matters and to take their Scotch and soda.
I am sorry I was not here last Saturday night. I did not think that the minister would take advantage of the small attendance of members at a Saturday night's sitting to get all his Estimates through. I wished to get some information with regard to the construction of the Connaught rifle range. I put a question on the Order Paper about the case of a young man named Healey, who was engaged to superintend the construction of cement walls. The minister said he was dismissed by his department. About forty bags of cement were found missing that were afterwards returned. It was very unjust, I will not say on the part of the minister, but of some officer, to put the blame on Healey, who was not the responsible party. Mr. Healey was engaged to superintend, first, the transportation of the cement from the station at South March to the works, a distance of about three miles, and Mr. Richardson, a good Conservative of Carle-ton, had the contract to transport that cement. Healey commenced to work in February, 1913, and, when the operations commenced in the spring, his duty was to superintend the mixing of cement. A Mr. Reid, a brother-in-law of Richardson, was constructing some concrete culverts, and

got short of cement. He borrowed about fifty bags of the cement which Mr. Richardson had the contract to convey to the works. That cement was afterwards returned by Mr. Reid, but the blame for its disappearance was put on Mr. Healey, who was dismissed on account of it. Mr. Healey is a respectable and honourable young man, and happens to be a L'.beral, which is so much the better for him. He never asked for the position; he was asked by the minister to take it. I think it was very unjust on the part of the minister, if he knew the facts, to put the blame on Mr. Healey and dismiss him, and to put a black mark against the name of this young man which will be on the records of Parliament foreveT.

Was it marl cement or
rock?

I am not sure about that. It whs to be used for building concrete walls. Mr. Healey told me that he was not on good terms with the foreman engaged by the contractors. They did not agree over the mixing of the cement. Healey insisted that more cement should he used in the construction than the foreman wanted. Healey also had difference with the engineer of the department and it may be that the engineer has made a report against him. But, if an investigation was held it could be proven that the engineer of the department had built a verandah to his summer house out of lumber belonging to the Government and also that Mr. Reid who was constructing the concrete culverts, employed a Mr. Thexton, an assistant engineer of the department, to draw the plans for these culverts and superintend their construction. I wish to put this on ' Hansard ' and I hope the minister will read it and do what is necessary in vindication of this young man Healey who has been so unjustly treated. I hope the minister will, read it, investigate the facts, and give a certificate of character to Mr. Healey.
